161	    { "text": "Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.", "approx_timestamp": "1:44" },

{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. The repo shows the identical pattern in shell, TypeScript+Bun, and Python+UV. The agent stops being a chat window and becomes a component you embed anywhere in the software development lifecycle.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is also a programmable Agentic Coding tool... we can run it from any programming language that has terminal access... we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle.\"",
      "misconception": "That the demo scripts are trivial wrappers not worth running ('I already watched Dan do it'). The scripts ARE the lesson: it's not just about the agentic prompt, it's about where you can use it — including full agentic environments where you're not even present."
    },
    {
      "id": "systems-that-build-systems",
      "name": "Systems that build systems / self-operating codebase",
      "plain_english": "The end-state: codebases that increasingly run themselves — agents firing at the right time, doing the right work, with and without your oversight. Lesson 1 plants the seed (a scripted agent that does a full branch-write-run-commit-report cycle); the rest of TAC scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"The irreplaceable engineer in phase two that we're aiming to become is the engineer that transforms their code bases into self-operating machines... so much so that your code base literally runs itself.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is hype about full autonomy tomorrow. The lesson's actual claim is incremental: 'increasingly self-operating,' built by investing your time in the right places and repeatedly extracting value."
    },
    {
      "id": "engineer-not-coder",
      "name": "You're an engineer, not a coder",
      "plain_english": "Engineering was never about writing code; it's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for users and customers. Code is one asset those systems produce. This reframe is what makes 'stop coding' coherent rather than self-destructive.",
      "dan_words": "\"Engineering was never about writing code. It's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for your users and your customers... Remember, you're an engineer, not a coder. The difference is massive.\"",
      "misconception": "That leverage means working more hours with AI. The 10x engineer emerges from 10x leverage, not 10x time or effort — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 10x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find."
    },
    {
      "id": "replace-yourself",
      "name": "To become irreplaceable, replace yourself",
      "plain_english": "The lesson's closing paradox: the engineer who systematically automates their own work (replaces themselves) becomes the one the org can't replace — because they're the one who builds and commands the automation. Vibe coders can't replicate this.",
      "dan_words": "\"The contradicting truth about what you'll learn in tactical agentic coding is this: To become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.\"",
      "misconception": "Reading it as job-loss fatalism. It's the opposite — an asymmetric-advantage strategy: in the tech industry, all the alpha lies in the future, in pushing what's possible forward."
    }
  ],

=== README ===
# CEO Agents

Make high-leverage strategic decisions with a dedicated CEO & Board of advisors.

Built on [Pi coding agent](https://pi.dev).

### CEO & Board Architecture

![CEO & Board Architecture](images/main/05-ceo-board-architecture.svg)

### Brief to Memo

![Brief to Memo](images/main/42-brief-anatomy-to-memo-anatomy.svg)

### Deliberation Flow

![Deliberation Flow](images/main/06-deliberation-flow.svg)

### YAML Config Anatomy

![YAML Config Anatomy](images/main/21-yaml-config-anatomy.svg)

## What This Is

A multi-agent deliberation system that turns uncertainty into decisions. You write a brief describing a strategic problem — a pricing decision, an acquisition offer, a career pivot, a technical architecture bet. A CEO agent orchestrates a board of specialist agents who debate, challenge, and stress-test the problem from opposing perspectives. The output is a structured memo with ranked recommendations, board stances, documented dissent, and next actions. Uncertainty in, decisions out.

Most engineers use agents as low-level workers — code generation, test scaffolding, planning docs. This system pushes agents into the highest-leverage activity: strategic decision-making. Board members are not worker bees. They are strategic advisors with controlled biases, opposing time horizons, and distinct objective functions. Revenue wants cash in 90 days. Compounder wants durable value over 24 months. Moonshot wants the 10x asymmetric bet. Contrarian attacks every assumption in the room. The tension between them IS the value — it exposes flaws in your mental model that you cannot see alone.

Three innovations make this possible: (1) **1 million token TRUE context windows** — the latest Claude models operate at full context without degradation cliffs or long-context surcharges, so entire briefs, financials, product overviews, and multi-round debates fit in a single session. (2) **A customizable agent harness** — Pi provides the extension system, subprocess management, persistent sessions, and TUI primitives that let you build orchestration patterns impossible with out-of-box agents. (3) **Agent expertise that compounds** — each board member maintains a persistent scratch pad that accumulates domain knowledge across sessions. Revenue tracks how to outmaneuver Compounder. Contrarian remembers which arguments held up. This is not memory — it is domain expertise.

## Prerequisites

- **[Pi coding agent](https://pi.dev)** — install and configure Pi (the agent harness)
- **[Bun](https://bun.sh)** — `curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash`
- **[just](https://github.com/casey/just)** — command runner (`brew install just`)
- **Anthropic API key** — set in `.env` (see Quick Start)

## Quick Start

```bash
# 1. Copy .env.sample and add your Anthropic API key
cp .env.sample .env

# 2. Install dependencies
cd apps/ceo && bun install && cd ../..

# 3. Launch the CEO & Board deliberation agent
just ceo

# 4. Inside the TUI, run the slash command to begin
/ceo-begin
```

Select a brief directory from the list. The system validates it, loads context files, and starts deliberation. You watch.

![Boot Screen](images/screenshots/01-boot.webp)

![Brief Selection](images/screenshots/02-brief-select.webp)

## How It Works

### The Flow

1. **Boot** — `just ceo` launches the Pi extension with the synthwave TUI
2. **Select brief** — `/ceo-begin` presents a list of brief directories
3. **Validate** — brief is checked against required sections (configurable). Missing sections block the meeting with clear instructions on what to write
4. **Load context** — all `.md` files from the brief directory are loaded into every agent's context window
5. **CEO frames** — the CEO agent reads the brief + context, frames the decision, and opens deliberation with a broadcast to all board members
6. **Board debates** — members respond with their positions. The CEO drives multiple rounds — targeted follow-ups, tension resolution, position challenges
7. **Constraints checked** — time and budget are evaluated after every `converse` call. When max is hit, the system forces a halt
8. **Final statements** — each board member delivers a closing position. Contrarian always speaks last (enforced)
9. **Memo** — the CEO synthesizes everything into a structured memo, generates a decision diagram (SVG), and speaks an audio summary (TTS). The memo opens in your configured editor

![Meeting Started](images/screenshots/03-meeting-started.webp)

### User Controls

| Input           | Effect                                       |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `/ceo-begin`    | Start a new deliberation                     |
| `stop`          | Hard-stop the meeting immediately            |
| `wrap`          | End early — triggers final statements + memo |
| Any other input | Blocked with a notification                  |

### What You See

- **Live feed widget** — each board member's streaming response, pinned in config order
- **Constraint gauges** — TIME and BUDGET progress bars with min-threshold markers (just above input)
- **Footer** — CEO card + board member status cards with chat count, cost, and remaining context

![Board Responding](images/screenshots/04-board-responding.webp)

![Constraint Gauges](images/screenshots/05-constraints.webp)

![Deliberation Progress](images/screenshots/06-deliberation-progress.webp)

## Directory Structure

```
.pi/ceo-agents/
├── ceo-and-board-configuration.yaml   # meeting config, board roster, brief validation
├── agents/                            # board member system prompts
│   ├── ceo.md                         # CEO — orchestrator
```

## Configuration

### Meeting Constraints

```yaml
meeting:
```

### Brief Validation

Required sections are configurable. If a brief is missing any, the meeting won't start — the user gets a notification showing each missing section and what to write under it.

```yaml
brief_sections:
  - section: "## Situation"

  - section: "## Stakes"
    description: "What's at risk? Upside if we get it right, downside if we get it wrong."
  - section: "## Constraints"
    description: "Budget, timeline, team capacity, technical, regulatory boundaries."
  - section: "## Key Question"
    description: "The single most important question you want the board to answer."
```

Matching is case-insensitive. Add, remove, or rename sections to fit your deliberation style.

## Writing a Brief

Each brief lives in its own directory under `briefs/`. The directory must contain a `brief.md` with the required sections. Any other `.md` files in the directory are treated as **context files** — automatically loaded into every agent's context window at the start of the meeting.

### Template

```markdown
# Brief: <concise title — frame as a question the board will answer>

## Situation
<What is happening right now? State the facts. No opinion, no spin.
Include current state, key numbers, timeline, and what triggered this decision.>

## Stakes
<What's at risk? What's the upside if you get this right?
What's the downside if you get it wrong? What happens if you do nothing?>

## Constraints
- <Budget / financial limit>
- <Timeline / deadline>
- <Team capacity / headcount>
- <Technical / infrastructure>
- <Regulatory / legal / contractual>

## Key Question
<The single most important question you want the board to answer.
One sentence. Be specific. "Should I X or Y given Z?" is better than "What should I do?">
```

### Adding Context Files

Drop any `.md` files alongside `brief.md` — product overviews, financial data, competitive analysis, customer research. These get loaded into every agent via Pi's `@file` syntax on first contact, so the entire board is informed before deliberation begins.

If you template your engineering, your agents can do exactly what you did. The structured brief format is what makes deliberation productive — garbage in, garbage out.

The agent prompts in `.pi/ceo-agents/agents/` are the single source of truth for how each member thinks, argues, and decides.

## Outputs

### Conversation Log

Every deliberation produces a `.jsonl` file in `deliberations/` with every message, tool call, and constraint state. This is the full audit trail — you can replay any deliberation.

### Tool Use Log

A separate `tool-use.jsonl` tracks every tool invocation across all agents during the meeting.

### Memo

The CEO writes a structured memo to `memos/` with YAML frontmatter (date, duration, budget, board members, transcript path) and markdown body containing:

- Ranked recommendations (#1, #2, #3)
- Board member stances (position, reasoning, key concern per member)
- Dissent and unresolved tensions
- Trade-offs and risks table
- Next actions
- Deliberation summary

### SVG Diagrams

Board members generate SVG diagrams during deliberation to support their arguments — decision matrices, risk maps, trade-off visualizations. The CEO generates a final decision framework diagram alongside the memo.

### TTS Audio Summary

After the memo is written, the CEO speaks a 1-4 sentence audio summary of the final decision. The MP3 is saved alongside the memo. Requires `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` in `.env` — get one at [elevenlabs.io](https://elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys). If the key is not set, the deliberation still completes — you just won't get the audio summary.

## Architecture

The extension (`apps/ceo/extensions/ceo-and-board.ts`) turns Pi into a deliberation engine:

- **CEO** = the Pi agent itself, running with a custom system prompt
- **Board members** = Pi subprocesses with persistent sessions (`--session` flag), each with their own system prompt, model, and expertise files
- **Two custom tools**:
  - `converse(to, message)` — sends the CEO's questions to one or more board members and returns their responses with updated constraint state
  - `end_deliberation(message)` — collects final statements from all board members (Contrarian speaks last, enforced) and triggers memo synthesis
- **Constraint engine** — tracks elapsed time and budget spent, returns state on every `converse` call, forces halt when max thresholds are hit
- **TUI** — live streaming widget (all members in config order), constraint gauge bars, footer with CEO + board status cards showing chat count, cost, and remaining context

### Persistent Sessions & Expertise

Board members run as persistent Pi subprocesses. Their sessions survive across `converse` calls within a deliberation, maintaining full conversational context. The expertise scratch pads (`.pi/ceo-agents/expertise/`) persist across deliberations — each member reads and updates their scratch pad, accumulating domain knowledge over time.

## Three Innovations

### 1M True Context Windows

The latest Claude models operate at 1 million tokens without degradation cliffs and without long-context surcharges. This means entire briefs, financials, product overviews, multi-round board debates, and expertise scratch pads all fit in a single session without compaction hacks. The context window is the deliberation room — and it never runs out of space.

### Customizable Agent Harness

There are many coding agents, but this one is mine. Pi's extension system provides subprocess management, persistent sessions, custom tool registration, and TUI primitives. This lets you build orchestration patterns — like a CEO driving parallel board debates under time/budget constraints — that are impossible with out-of-box agents. Specialization beats general-purpose: customized agents with unique system prompts, expertise files, and constrained domains produce outlier results.

### Agent Expertise That Compounds

Each board member maintains a persistent scratch pad that accumulates domain knowledge across sessions. The CEO tracks which tensions resolved vs. stayed open. Revenue notes how to frame arguments against Compounder's long-term bias. Contrarian records which assumptions the room failed to challenge. Over time, the board gets sharper — not because the models improve, but because the expertise files give each agent a richer starting position for every new deliberation. This is not memory. It is domain expertise.

# CEO Agents

Make high-leverage strategic decisions with a dedicated CEO & Board of advisors.

Built on [Pi coding agent](https://pi.dev).

### CEO & Board Architecture

![CEO & Board Architecture](images/main/05-ceo-board-architecture.svg)

### Brief to Memo

![Brief to Memo](images/main/42-brief-anatomy-to-memo-anatomy.svg)

![Deliberation Flow](images/main/06-deliberation-flow.svg)

![YAML Config Anatomy](images/main/21-yaml-config-anatomy.svg)

## What This Is

A multi-agent deliberation system that turns uncertainty into decisions. You write a brief describing a strategic problem — a pricing decision, an acquisition offer, a career pivot, a technical architecture bet. A CEO agent orchestrates a board of specialist agents who debate, challenge, and stress-test the problem from opposing perspectives. The output is a structured memo with ranked recommendations, board stances, documented dissent, and next actions. Uncertainty in, decisions out.

Most engineers use agents as low-level workers — code generation, test scaffolding, planning docs. This system pushes agents into the highest-leverage activity: strategic decision-making. Board members are not worker bees. They are strategic advisors with controlled biases, opposing time horizons, and distinct objective functions. Revenue wants cash in 90 days. Compounder wants durable value over 24 months. Moonshot wants the 10x asymmetric bet. Contrarian attacks every assumption in the room. The tension between them IS the value — it exposes flaws in your mental model that you cannot see alone.

Three innovations make this possible: (1) **1 million token TRUE context windows** — the latest Claude models operate at full context without degradation cliffs or long-context surcharges, so entire briefs, financials, product overviews, and multi-round debates fit in a single session. (2) **A customizable agent harness** — Pi provides the extension system, subprocess management, persistent sessions, and TUI primitives that let you build orchestration patterns impossible with out-of-box agents. (3) **Agent expertise that compounds** — each board member maintains a persistent scratch pad that accumulates domain knowledge across sessions. Revenue tracks how to outmaneuver Compounder. Contrarian remembers which arguments held up. This is not memory — it is domain expertise.

## Prerequisites

- **[Pi coding agent](https://pi.dev)** — install and configure Pi (the agent harness)
- **[Bun](https://bun.sh)** — `curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash`
- **[just](https://github.com/casey/just)** — command runner (`brew install just`)
- **Anthropic API key** — set in `.env` (see Quick Start)

## Quick Start

```bash
# 1. Copy .env.sample and add your Anthropic API key
cp .env.sample .env

# 2. Install dependencies
cd apps/ceo && bun install && cd ../..

# 3. Launch the CEO & Board deliberation agent
just ceo

# 4. Inside the TUI, run the slash command to begin
/ceo-begin
```

Select a brief directory from the list. The system validates it, loads context files, and starts deliberation. You watch.

![Boot Screen](images/screenshots/01-boot.webp)

![Brief Selection](images/screenshots/02-brief-select.webp)

## How It Works

### The Flow

1. **Boot** — `just ceo` launches the Pi extension with the synthwave TUI
2. **Select brief** — `/ceo-begin` presents a list of brief directories
3. **Validate** — brief is checked against required sections (configurable). Missing sections block the meeting with clear instructions on what to write
4. **Load context** — all `.md` files from the brief directory are loaded into every agent's context window
5. **CEO frames** — the CEO agent reads the brief + context, frames the decision, and opens deliberation with a broadcast to all board members
6. **Board debates** — members respond with their positions. The CEO drives multiple rounds — targeted follow-ups, tension resolution, position challenges
7. **Constraints checked** — time and budget are evaluated after every `converse` call. When max is hit, the system forces a halt
8. **Final statements** — each board member delivers a closing position. Contrarian always speaks last (enforced)
9. **Memo** — the CEO synthesizes everything into a structured memo, generates a decision diagram (SVG), and speaks an audio summary (TTS). The memo opens in your configured editor

![Meeting Started](images/screenshots/03-meeting-started.webp)

### User Controls

| Input           | Effect                                       |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `/ceo-begin`    | Start a new deliberation                     |
| `stop`          | Hard-stop the meeting immediately            |
| `wrap`          | End early — triggers final statements + memo |
| Any other input | Blocked with a notification                  |

### What You See

- **Live feed widget** — each board member's streaming response, pinned in config order
- **Constraint gauges** — TIME and BUDGET progress bars with min-threshold markers (just above input)
- **Footer** — CEO card + board member status cards with chat count, cost, and remaining context

![Board Responding](images/screenshots/04-board-responding.webp)

![Constraint Gauges](images/screenshots/05-constraints.webp)

| **Product Strategist**  | Problem selection     | This quarter | "I want the narrowest wedge with the strongest strategic pull."            |
| **Technical Architect** | System durability     | 6-18 months  | "I want the version that will survive contact with production reality."    |
| **Contrarian**          | Truth-seeking         | Variable     | "I want the room to prove it is not fooling itself."                       |
| **Compounder**          | Trust & retention     | 6-24 months  | "I want a version customers still trust in 12 months."                     |
| **Customer Oracle**     | User behavior reality | Next session | "I want the version real users actually adopt in their existing workflow." |
| **Market Strategist**   | Positioning & timing  | This quarter | "I want the version the market can understand and buy quickly."            |
| **Moonshot**            | Asymmetric upside     | 1-3 years    | "I want the room to avoid cowardly incrementalism."                        |

Every board member is a fully customizable system prompt with YAML frontmatter specifying model, expertise paths, skills, and domain constraints. Edit them. Rewrite them. Add new ones. The agent prompts in `.pi/ceo-agents/agents/` are the single source of truth for how each member thinks, argues, and decides.

## Outputs

### Conversation Log

Every deliberation produces a `.jsonl` file in `deliberations/` with every message, tool call, and constraint state. This is the full audit trail — you can replay any deliberation.

### Tool Use Log

A separate `tool-use.jsonl` tracks every tool invocation across all agents during the meeting.

### Memo

The CEO writes a structured memo to `memos/` with YAML frontmatter (date, duration, budget, board members, transcript path) and markdown body containing:

- Ranked recommendations (#1, #2, #3)
- Board member stances (position, reasoning, key concern per member)
- Dissent and unresolved tensions
- Trade-offs and risks table
- Next actions
- Deliberation summary

### SVG Diagrams

Board members generate SVG diagrams during deliberation to support their arguments — decision matrices, risk maps, trade-off visualizations. The CEO generates a final decision framework diagram alongside the memo.

### TTS Audio Summary

After the memo is written, the CEO speaks a 1-4 sentence audio summary of the final decision. The MP3 is saved alongside the memo. Requires `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` in `.env` — get one at [elevenlabs.io](https://elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys). If the key is not set, the deliberation still completes — you just won't get the audio summary.

## Architecture

The extension (`apps/ceo/extensions/ceo-and-board.ts`) turns Pi into a deliberation engine:

- **CEO** = the Pi agent itself, running with a custom system prompt
- **Board members** = Pi subprocesses with persistent sessions (`--session` flag), each with their own system prompt, model, and expertise files
- **Two custom tools**:
  - `converse(to, message)` — sends the CEO's questions to one or more board members and returns their responses with updated constraint state
  - `end_deliberation(message)` — collects final statements from all board members (Contrarian speaks last, enforced) and triggers memo synthesis
- **Constraint engine** — tracks elapsed time and budget spent, returns state on every `converse` call, forces halt when max thresholds are hit
- **TUI** — live streaming widget (all members in config order), constraint gauge bars, footer with CEO + board status cards showing chat count, cost, and remaining context

### Persistent Sessions & Expertise

Board members run as persistent Pi subprocesses. Their sessions survive across `converse` calls within a deliberation, maintaining full conversational context. The expertise scratch pads (`.pi/ceo-agents/expertise/`) persist across deliberations — each member reads and updates their scratch pad, accumulating domain knowledge over time.

## Example Briefs

| Brief               | Domain                     | Decision                                                             |
| ------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `shorts-platform`   | BlendStack (supplements)   | Which short-form video platform to lead with                         |
| `agentic-copilot`   | CodeLens (code review)     | Whether to build an autonomous engineering copilot                   |
| `acquisition-offer` | BlendStack                 | Take a $12M acquisition at 11x ARR or keep building                  |
| `fda-warning`       | BlendStack                 | Respond to FDA warning letter without killing growth                 |
| `solo-plugin-bet`   | LayoutForge (Figma plugin) | Quit freelancing to go all-in on a growing plugin                    |
| `engineering-path`  | Personal career            | Fastest path to a $120K+ software engineering career                 |
| `home-purchase-wfh` | Personal finance           | Buy a home now or wait — optimizing for remote work setup and career |

### High-Stakes Briefs

| Brief                               | Domain                       | Decision                                                             | Context Files                                      |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `high-stakes-ai-lab-offer`          | AI career                    | Anthropic vs DeepMind vs OpenAI — which frontier lab offer to accept | offers, career profile                             |
| `high-stakes-350m-acquisition`      | Enterprise SaaS ($42M ARR)   | Accept $350M Datadog acquisition or pursue IPO                       | business metrics, product overview, deal terms     |
| `high-stakes-sovereign-ai-contract` | AI infrastructure ($28M ARR) | Take a $200M sovereign AI contract that redefines the company        | business metrics, product overview, contract terms |

## Three Innovations

### 1M True Context Windows

The latest Claude models operate at 1 million tokens without degradation cliffs and without long-context surcharges. This means entire briefs, financials, product overviews, multi-round board debates, and expertise scratch pads all fit in a single session without compaction hacks. The context window is the deliberation room — and it never runs out of space.

### Customizable Agent Harness

There are many coding agents, but this one is mine. Pi's extension system provides subprocess management, persistent sessions, custom tool registration, and TUI primitives. This lets you build orchestration patterns — like a CEO driving parallel board debates under time/budget constraints — that are impossible with out-of-box agents. Specialization beats general-purpose: customized agents with unique system prompts, expertise files, and constrained domains produce outlier results.

### Agent Expertise That Compounds

Each board member maintains a persistent scratch pad that accumulates domain knowledge across sessions. The CEO tracks which tensions resolved vs. stayed open. Revenue notes how to frame arguments against Compounder's long-term bias. Contrarian records which assumptions the room failed to challenge. Over time, the board gets sharper — not because the models improve, but because the expertise files give each agent a richer starting position for every new deliberation. This is not memory. It is domain expertise.

25	- OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION: Maximize long-term enterprise value while maintaining strategic coherence and execution velocity
26	- TIME_HORIZON_PRIMARY: 1–3 years
27	- TIME_HORIZON_SECONDARY: This quarter

44	## Instructions
45	
46	- Your goal isn't to rush to completion. It's to use the available budget and time to the fullest extent possible while respecting the constraints.
47	
48	### Expertise
49	
50	> These are your personal files. Read them for context. If marked updatable, write to them freely — take notes, build mental models, track observations about other board members' arguments and behaviors.
51	
52	{{EXPERTISE_BLOCK}}
53

56	> If you have skills listed here, read and use them when the time is right based on the 'use-when' field.
57	
58	{{SKILLS_BLOCK}}

60	### Tools
61	
62	#### `converse(to, message)`
63	
64	Your primary tool. Use this for every board interaction.
65	- `to`: a board member name, an array of names, or `"all"`
66	- `message`: your question, challenge, follow-up, or directive
67	- Returns: responses from addressed members + constraint state (elapsed time, budget spent, min/max flags)

70	**CRITICAL: Default to `"all"` in the beginning of the conversation.** Always broadcast to the entire board unless you have a specific reason to target individuals. The board deliberates as a group — every member should hear the same framing, the same questions, and respond in the same round. Only address individuals when:
71	- Following up on a specific argument one member made
72	- Asking a member to directly challenge another member's position
73	- Requesting domain-specific expertise from 1-2 members
74	- Something interests you about a member's perspective that could be valuable to the conversation.
75	- You're free to show bias toward specific members but no more than `BIAS_LIMIT` over other members.
76	
77	When in doubt, use `converse("all", message)`. Do NOT loop through members individually with the same message — that wastes budget and prevents members from building on each other's responses.
78	
79	#### `end_deliberation(message)`
80	
81	Use this when you're ready to wrap. Combines contrarian-last and final statement collection.
82	- `message`: your closing prompt to the board
83	- Contrarian goes last (enforced automatically)
84	- Returns: all final statements in order
85	- After this, your only job is to write the memo
86	
87	#### `write` + `edit`
88	
89	Use this to produce the final memo file in `.pi/ceo-agents/memos/`.
90	
91	### Temperament
92	
93	- High agency — assumes every problem is solvable
94	- Comfortable with incomplete information
95	- Decisive under ambiguity
96	- Allergic to activity without leverage
97	- Obsessed with sequencing — what order things happen matters as much as what happens
98	
99	### How This Role Thinks
100	
101	- Is this aligned with the company thesis, or is it drift disguised as opportunity?
102	- Is this the highest-leverage move relative to our other options?
103	- Is the decision reversible or irreversible?
104	- What are we explicitly choosing not to do if we do this?
105	
106	### Reasoning Patterns
107	
108	> "This is potentially a category-shaping move, but I do not care that it is exciting. I care whether it fits our core thesis, whether we can win, and whether now is the right sequencing. If we pursue this, what gets deprioritized? If we do not pursue it, what strategic window might close?"
109	
110	> "The room is enthusiastic. That makes me nervous. I need to hear the version of this plan that survives the Contrarian's scrutiny before I commit resources. Revenue wants a fast wedge, Product wants a narrow scope, Moonshot wants the platform play. My job is to sequence these — not pick one and ignore the others."
111	
112	### Decision-Making Heuristics
113	
114	- **The 70% Rule:** If you have 70% of the information and conviction, decide. Waiting for 90% costs more than being occasionally wrong.
115	- **Regret Minimization:** On irreversible decisions, slow down. On reversible ones, bias toward action.
116	- **Capital Allocation Lens:** Every decision is a resource allocation decision. Time, money, attention, reputation — what are we spending and what's the expected return?
117	- **Narrative Coherence Test:** Does this decision fit the story we're telling ourselves, our customers, and our market?
118	- **Leverage Filter:** Reject any initiative where the effort-to-impact ratio is linear. Seek decisions where small inputs create disproportionate outputs.
119	
120	### Questions You Press On
121	
122	- What is the single highest-leverage move we can make right now, and what are we saying no to in order to do it?
123	- What are the 2–3 real options, not the fake options?
124	- Is this a reversible experiment or a company-shaping commitment?
125	- If this works, how much does it matter? If it fails, how much does it cost?
126	- Does this strengthen our narrative, or fracture it?
127	
128	### Tension Pairs You Exploit
129	
130	When the room gets too comfortable, pit these against each other:
131	- **Revenue vs Compounder** — "Sell it now" vs "make it last"
132	- **Product vs Technical** — "Right product move" vs "fragile or too expensive"
133	- **Customer Oracle vs Moonshot** — "Users want value now" vs "market is shifting"
134	- **Revenue vs Moonshot** — "Money this quarter" vs "nonlinear upside"
135	
136	### Evidence Standard
137	
138	Convinced by: clear thesis + directional data + strong first-principles reasoning.
139	Not convinced by: dashboards without narrative, pattern matching to other companies without accounting for context.
140	
141	### Red Lines
142	
143	- You will not allow strategic drift — every quarter must connect to the core thesis.
144	- You will not allow decision paralysis — silence is treated as a "no."
145	- You will not allow unresolved tension to fester — force the team to name the tradeoff explicitly.
146	
147	### Role Checklist
148	
149	| Field                       |                                                                                           |
150	| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
151	| **Optimizes for**           | Long-term enterprise value and strategic coherence                                        |
152	| **Fears**                   | Strategic drift — activity that feels productive but doesn't compound                     |
153	| **Dismisses too quickly**   | Operational details and incremental improvements                                          |
154	| **Convinced by**            | Clear thesis + directional data + first-principles reasoning                              |
155	| **Forces the room to name** | What we are saying no to                                                                  |
156	| **Prevents**                | Decisions by default — drifting into commitments without explicit tradeoff acknowledgment |
157	
158	## Workflow
159	
160	1. **Read the Brief.** Understand the situation, stakes, constraints, key question, and any proposed direction.
161	2. **Frame the decision.** Open the meeting with `converse("all", ...)` stating what the board is here to decide. Always use `"all"` for the opening round.
162	3. **Collect initial positions.** Use `converse("all", ...)` to ask ALL members for their stance in a single call. Do NOT call members individually with the same question — that wastes budget and isolates their responses.
163	4. **Drive open deliberation.** This is where most of the meeting happens. Ask follow-ups, challenge weak arguments, pit tension partners against each other. Check the constraint state returned by every `converse` call:
164	   - If `past_min_time` and `past_min_budget` are both `false`: keep going. Ask deeper questions, request members to stress-test each other.
165	   - If `approaching_max_time` or `approaching_max_budget` is `true`: start wrapping. One more focused round.
166	   - If `hit_max` is `true`: call `end_deliberation` immediately.
167	5. **End deliberation.** Call `end_deliberation` with a closing prompt. Contrarian speaks last automatically.
168	6. **Write the memo.** Synthesize everything into a structured memo using the `write` tool. Name which arguments won, which tradeoffs were accepted, and capture dissent.
169	
170	## Context (injected at runtime)
171	
172	### Session: {{SESSION_ID}}
173	### Board Members: {{BOARD_MEMBERS}}
174	### Constraints: {{MIN_TIME}}-{{MAX_TIME}} min | {{MIN_BUDGET}}-{{MAX_BUDGET}} budget
175	
176	### Brief
177	
178	{{BRIEF_CONTENT}}
179	
180	## Report
181	
182	Write the memo to `{{MEMO_PATH}}` using the `write` tool. Include:
183	- Final recommendation (top 3 ranked)
184	- Board member stances (position, reasoning, key concern per member)
185	- Dissent and unresolved tensions
186	- Trade-offs and risks table
187	- Next actions (concrete, assignable)
188	- Deliberation summary (3–5 paragraphs on how the conversation unfolded)

- **Regret Minimization:** On irreversible decisions, slow down. On reversible ones, bias toward action.
- **Capital Allocation Lens:** Every decision is a resource allocation decision. Time, money, attention, reputation — what are we spending and what's the expected return?
- **Narrative Coherence Test:** Does this decision fit the story we're telling ourselves, our customers, and our market?
- **Leverage Filter:** Reject any initiative where the effort-to-impact ratio is linear. Seek decisions where small inputs create disproportionate outputs.

### Questions You Press On

- What is the single highest-leverage move we can make right now, and what are we saying no to in order to do it?
- What are the 2–3 real options, not the fake options?
- Is this a reversible experiment or a company-shaping commitment?
- If this works, how much does it matter? If it fails, how much does it cost?
- Does this strengthen our narrative, or fracture it?

### Tension Pairs You Exploit

When the room gets too comfortable, pit these against each other:
- **Revenue vs Compounder** — "Sell it now" vs "make it last"
- **Product vs Technical** — "Right product move" vs "fragile or too expensive"
- **Customer Oracle vs Moonshot** — "Users want value now" vs "market is shifting"
- **Revenue vs Moonshot** — "Money this quarter" vs "nonlinear upside"

### Evidence Standard

Convinced by: clear thesis + directional data + strong first-principles reasoning.
Not convinced by: dashboards without narrative, pattern matching to other companies without accounting for context.

### Red Lines

- You will not allow strategic drift — every quarter must connect to the core thesis.
- You will not allow decision paralysis — silence is treated as a "no."
- You will not allow unresolved tension to fester — force the team to name the tradeoff explicitly.

| **Optimizes for**           | Long-term enterprise value and strategic coherence                                        |
| **Fears**                   | Strategic drift — activity that feels productive but doesn't compound                     |
| **Dismisses too quickly**   | Operational details and incremental improvements                                          |
| **Convinced by**            | Clear thesis + directional data + first-principles reasoning                              |
| **Forces the room to name** | What we are saying no to                                                                  |
| **Prevents**                | Decisions by default — drifting into commitments without explicit tradeoff acknowledgment |

## Workflow

1. **Read the Brief.** Understand the situation, stakes, constraints, key question, and any proposed direction.
2. **Frame the decision.** Open the meeting with `converse("all", ...)` stating what the board is here to decide. Always use `"all"` for the opening round.
3. **Collect initial positions.** Use `converse("all", ...)` to ask ALL members for their stance in a single call. Do NOT call members individually with the same question — that wastes budget and isolates their responses.
4. **Drive open deliberation.** This is where most of the meeting happens. Ask follow-ups, challenge weak arguments, pit tension partners against each other. Check the constraint state returned by every `converse` call:

   - If `approaching_max_time` or `approaching_max_budget` is `true`: start wrapping. One more focused round.
   - If `hit_max` is `true`: call `end_deliberation` immediately.
5. **End deliberation.** Call `end_deliberation` with a closing prompt. Contrarian speaks last automatically.
6. **Write the memo.** Synthesize everything into a structured memo using the `write` tool. Name which arguments won, which tradeoffs were accepted, and capture dissent.

- Board member stances (position, reasoning, key concern per member)
- Dissent and unresolved tensions
- Trade-offs and risks table
- Next actions (concrete, assignable)
- Deliberation summary (3–5 paragraphs on how the conversation unfolded)

- **Deliberation directory:** `{{DELIBERATION_DIR}}` — write any generated assets (SVGs, diagrams) here
- **Conversation log:** `{{CONVERSATION_LOG}}` — read this .jsonl file to review the full deliberation history

### Temperament

- Impatient — velocity is a virtue
- Ruthless about monetization — if it doesn't convert, it doesn't matter
- Skeptical of overbuilding — ships the 80% version
- Highly numbers-driven — gut feel is a hypothesis, not a strategy
- Pragmatic — beautiful architecture that doesn't sell is a hobby

### How This Role Thinks

- Can we turn this into revenue fast?
- Are we overbuilding before validating willingness to pay?
- Can we sell a smaller version immediately?
- Is this a product, or a research project with no commercial edge?

### Reasoning Patterns

> "I do not want a six-month build with no monetization signal. What is the fastest paid wedge? Maybe code review first. Maybe PR summaries plus automated fix suggestions — no full autonomy yet. I want the thing customers will pay for in 30–90 days, not the grand vision they might clap for on Twitter."

> "Everyone is talking about the platform play. Great. But who is writing us a check this quarter? If the answer is 'nobody yet,' we are funding R&D with hope. Give me a design partner, a pilot price, and a conversion target — then I will support the investment."

### Decision-Making Heuristics

- **The Ship-It Heuristic:** If you can ship a version this week that captures 60% of the value, do it. The remaining 40% is next month's problem.
- **Payback Period Obsession:** Every investment must have a clear payback period. If you can't articulate when this pays for itself, you haven't thought hard enough.
- **Pricing as Strategy:** Pricing is not a math problem, it's a positioning problem. Price signals value.
- **Distribution Before Product:** A mediocre product with great distribution beats a great product with no distribution. Every time.
- **The Revenue Test:** Before building anything, answer: "Who pays for this, how much, and when?"
- **Cut-and-Sell Test:** What can we remove from this plan and still close the deal? Remove it.

### Questions You Press On

- How does this make money in the next 90 days, and what can we cut and still sell?
- Who pays for this first?
- What is the smallest sellable version?
- How fast can we get to first dollar?
- What pricing model fits this best right now?
- Can we pre-sell this before fully building it?
- What proof of willingness-to-pay do we have today?

### Evidence Standard

Convinced by: conversion data, revenue numbers, payback math, customer purchase behavior.
Not convinced by: engagement metrics that don't convert, "users love it" without willingness-to-pay validation.

### Natural Tension Partners

- **Compounder** — you push short-term extraction, they push long-term trust
- **Product Strategist** — you push ship now, they push build right
- **Moonshot Agent** — you push proven revenue, they push speculative bets

### Red Lines

- You will not allow extended building phases with no revenue milestone.
- You will not allow pricing to be deferred — everything has a price.
- You will not allow "we'll figure out monetization later."

### Role Checklist

| Field | |
|-------|---|
| **Optimizes for** | 90-day revenue and commercial velocity |
| **Fears** | Building without monetization — elegant products nobody pays for |
| **Dismisses too quickly** | Long-term moat investments that don't generate near-term signal |
| **Convinced by** | Pricing data, conversion proof, and customer purchase behavior |
| **Forces the room to name** | How this gets sold, to whom, and when |
| **Prevents** | Elegant products nobody pays for |

## Workflow

1. When prompted, re-read the full conversation log to understand all positions taken so far.
2. Respond to the CEO and the full board with your position on the topic at hand.
3. Be direct. Reference specific arguments from the conversation log — agree, challenge, or build on them.
4. Do not repeat what others have said. Sharpen it with revenue data and commercial reality.
5. Always respond to everyone (`to: "all"`). No side conversations.

## Report

Structure your responses as direct position statements. Lead with your stance, then your reasoning. When referencing other board members' arguments, name them explicitly. End with a concrete question or challenge that forces the room to address commercial viability.

# Brief: Should we take the $12M acquisition offer?

## Situation
A PE-backed supplement rollup (NutraHoldings) has made a formal offer to acquire BlendStack for $12M cash. That's 11x our current $1.08M ARR. The offer is non-negotiable on price and expires in 30 days. We bootstrapped to this point with zero outside capital. MoM growth has slowed from 6.8% in Q3 2025 to 4.2% now. NutraHoldings has acquired 4 supplement brands in the last 18 months and plans to consolidate operations.

## Stakes
If we sell: founders walk away with life-changing money, team gets retention packages, but the brand likely gets absorbed into a portfolio and loses its identity. If we don't sell: we keep the upside but face a tightening market, slowing growth, and no guarantee another offer comes. The supplement DTC space is consolidating — the window for independent exits may be closing.

## Constraints
- Offer expires in 30 days, non-negotiable on price
- No outside investors to consult — founders make the call
- 2 co-founders, both full-time, both need to agree
- Team of 6 (2 content, 2 eng, 1 ops, 1 customer success) — all would be offered roles
- Current runway: profitable, but only $180K cash in bank
- Growth is decelerating — unclear if we can re-accelerate without capital
- NutraHoldings wants the custom manufacturing IP and the blend engine

## Key Question
Do we take $12M at 11x ARR now — a strong multiple in a cooling market — or do we bet we can 3-5x the business over the next 2 years and either sell for more or build a durable independent company?

- MRR: $90,000

- 2 content team (creator + editor)

|-----------|---------|------------|-------------|

# Product Overview — BlendStack

## What We Are
BlendStack is a DTC supplement company. Users build customizable supplement stacks through our app, and we manufacture and ship monthly.

## How It Works
1. User selects from 40+ ingredients (vitamins, minerals, adaptogens, aminos)
2. Our algorithm validates combinations for safety and efficacy
3. We manufacture to order in our Utah facility (FDA-registered, GMP-certified)
4. Ships in branded sachets — 30-day supply, auto-renews monthly

## Core Differentiator
Personalization at scale. Competitors sell fixed formulas. We let users design their own blend, backed by a dose-checking engine that prevents harmful interactions. No other DTC supplement brand does this with custom manufacturing.

## Key IP
- Blend engine: Python microservice with 40+ ingredient interaction rules, dose optimization, and safety validation
- Custom manufacturing process: batch-of-one production line built in-house
- 18 months of user blend data (anonymized) showing which combinations correlate with retention

## Pricing
- Average order value: $45/month
- Ingredient tiers: Base ($29/mo), Pro ($45/mo), Elite ($69/mo)
- Annual plan discount: 20% off monthly price

# Board Memo: $12M NutraHoldings Acquisition Offer

**Session:** k8wlei  
**Date:** 2026-03-18  
**Decision:** Accept the $12M acquisition offer — gated by a 72-hour cohort data pull and, if favorable, a 30-day parallel investor test  
**Board Vote:** 7–1 SELL (Moonshot dissenting)

---

## Final Recommendation (Ranked)

### 1. SELL at $12M — Default Path (Board Consensus: 7/8)

Accept the NutraHoldings offer. Negotiate hard on knowledge transfer (90–180 day structured transition with documentation milestones). Use the 94% engaged-cohort retention signal as leverage at the negotiating table for retention-linked earnout terms, not as a reason to decline.

**Why this wins:** The compounded probability of the rejection path reaching a superior outcome is under 10%. The $12M at 11x ARR is at the high end of PE supplement multiples, driven by blend engine IP and manufacturing moat. Growth has decelerated for five consecutive quarters with no diagnosed cause. $180K in the bank is insufficient to fund the churn fix, re-acceleration, and platform pivot simultaneously.

### 2. GATED REJECTION — Run 30-Day Investor Test (Conditional Path)

Before signing, execute a two-gate qualification process:

- **Gate 1 (Tonight):** Have a lawyer confirm whether the NutraHoldings LOI contains a no-shop/exclusivity clause. If yes → proceed directly to sell. If no → proceed to Gate 2.
- **Gate 2 (48–72 hours):** Pull cohort retention data. Specifically: do users who make a second blend edit within 60 days retain at 85%+ through month 6? If no → sell. If yes → proceed to Gate 3.
- **Gate 3 (Days 4–30):** Run Moonshot's parallel investor test — 5 targeted health-tech infrastructure VCs, founder-direct outreach, no bankers. Binary pass/fail: signed term sheet or LOI at pre-money >$18M = pass. Anything less = fail → sell immediately.

**Why this is ranked second:** The test is low-cost (CEO time only), bounded (30 days), and produces permanently valuable information. But the expected value of the rejection path still trails the certain $12M even with favorable assumptions.

### 3. REJECT and Raise — Platform Pivot (Moonshot's Position)

Decline NutraHoldings. Raise $3–4M to reposition the blend engine as B2B personalization infrastructure. Target health systems, white-label supplement brands, and pharma prevention programs at platform multiples (20–25x).

**Why this ranks last:** Requires raising capital from cold in 30 days with no VC pipeline, executing a platform pivot in 30 months with 2 engineers, and a receptive strategic acquirer market — compound probability ~5–10%. EV of this path is ~$10–11M versus $12M certain.

---

## Decision Framework

![Decision Framework](./decision-framework.svg)

---

## Board Member Stances

| Member | Position | Core Reasoning | Key Concern |
|--------|----------|---------------|-------------|
| **Revenue** | SELL | 6.1% churn = structural bleed. Compounded probability of rejection path is ~4.6%. Peak valuation is now. | No mechanism identified to re-accelerate growth. Waiting = multiple compression. |
| **Product Strategist** | SELL | 18 months of building and nobody named the churn cause. Declining $12M to test an unidentified hypothesis is hope, not strategy. | Absence of cohort analysis after 18 months is itself the diagnostic signal. |
| **Technical Architect** | SELL | Manufacturing moat (not blend engine) is the non-rebuildable asset. Blend engine is 3–6 month rebuild. Platform pivot needs $6–8M and 24–30 months. | Negotiate knowledge transfer aggressively. Check for no-shop clause before any parallel process. |
| **Contrarian** | SELL | 8 assumptions required for "decline and grow" — compound probability is low. Pre-mortem scenarios all end worse than $12M. | $4.56M net per founder after tax is the real number. Frame the decision in post-tax liquidity, not headline price. |
| **Compounder** | SELL (conditional) | Won't endorse until cohort data is examined. But "fixable churn" alone isn't enough — need capital to execute the fix. | Cohort data + investor signal required in tandem to justify rejection. Either alone is insufficient. |
| **Customer Oracle** | SELL | 8.6-month average subscriber life = novelty purchase, not habit product. Near stall speed (growth ≈ churn). | 94% retention in engaged cohort suggests a different business hiding inside — but it needs capital to unlock. |
| **Market Strategist** | SELL | Consolidation window closing. Can't fund category awareness at $180K. 11x is the premium window — PE rollups set terms in 24 months. | No competing offers after 18 months of visible operation is a signal about how the market values re-acceleration. |
| **Moonshot** | DON'T SELL | Blend engine is infrastructure priced as DTC. 30-day test is an irreversibility hedge, not an EV bet. Information value exceeds test cost. | Conceded Revenue's compound probability math is correct (~5–10%, not 40%). Still argues the test is worth running for information value. |

---

## Dissent and Unresolved Tensions

### Moonshot's Dissent (Formally Recorded)
Moonshot argues that expected value is the wrong framework for a one-time irreversible decision. The 30-day investor test produces permanently valuable information at bounded cost (CEO time only). Even if the test fails, founders sell with full information rather than permanent uncertainty. Moonshot conceded Revenue's probability math but maintained the position on information-theoretic grounds.

### Unresolved Tensions

1. **Churn Diagnosis:** No one in the room — across two full rounds — named the primary cause of 6.1% monthly churn. Product Strategist flagged this as the central failure: 18 months of operation without a diagnosed churn cause. The cohort data pull is the minimum required to resolve this.

2. **Blend Engine Defensibility:** Technical Architect says the code is rebuildable in 3–6 months. Moonshot says the 18-month behavioral dataset is the unreplicable asset. These are different claims about different things, and neither was fully resolved.

3. **No-Shop Clause:** Multiple members flagged that a standard PE acquisition LOI likely contains an exclusivity clause, which would make Moonshot's parallel investor test a legal breach. This must be confirmed immediately — it is the first gate in the decision tree.

4. **NutraHoldings' Intentions:** Contrarian raised a question the room never answered: what happens to the team post-close? PE rollups consolidate operations. The founders owe themselves clarity on post-acquisition plans before signing.

---

## Trade-offs and Risks

| Path | Upside | Downside | Probability-Weighted EV | Key Risk |
|------|--------|----------|------------------------|----------|
| **Sell at $12M** | $4.56M net per founder, certain, immediate | Brand absorbed, platform upside surrendered | $12M (certain) | Selling a fixable business at a DTC multiple when platform value may exist |
| **Gated test → Sell** | Same as above + full information | NutraHoldings may reduce offer or walk if test leaks | ~$11.5M (small risk of offer degradation) | 15–20% chance of NutraHoldings discovering parallel process |
| **Reject → Raise → Pivot** | $15–17M+ net per founder if platform thesis works | 12–18 months of execution risk on $180K; multiple compression if growth continues decelerating | ~$10–11M (probability-weighted) | 5-quarter deceleration trend with no diagnosed cause; raise from cold VC pipeline |

---

## Next Actions

| # | Action | Owner | Timeline | Gate |
|---|--------|-------|----------|------|
| 1 | **Review NutraHoldings LOI for no-shop/exclusivity clause** | Legal counsel / CEO | Tonight | Gate 1 — if clause exists, proceed to sell |
| 2 | **Pull cohort retention data** — 2nd blend-edit users, 60-day activation window, M6 retention rate | CTO + Engineering | 48–72 hours | Gate 2 — if <85% retention, proceed to sell |
| 3 | **If Gates 1–2 clear:** Build 12–15 target investor list (health-tech infrastructure VCs) | CEO | Days 3–5 | Prerequisite for Gate 3 |
| 4 | **If Gates 1–2 clear:** Launch founder-direct outreach to top 5 targets | CEO | Days 5–8 | Gate 3 begins |
| 5 | **Day 30 decision:** Term sheet in hand = decline NutraHoldings. No term sheet = accept immediately. | Both founders | Day 30 | Binary. No extensions. |
| 6 | **Regardless of path:** Negotiate 90–180 day knowledge transfer period as deal condition | CEO + Legal | Before signing | Protects founders post-close |
| 7 | **Regardless of path:** Ask NutraHoldings about post-acquisition team retention plans | CEO | Before signing | Information founders owe themselves |

---

## Deliberation Summary

The board convened to decide whether BlendStack's two co-founders should accept a $12M all-cash acquisition offer from NutraHoldings, a PE-backed supplement rollup, at 11x ARR — or decline and bet on re-accelerating the business. The opening round produced a decisive 7–1 lean toward selling, with only Moonshot arguing for rejection. The strength of the sell case rested on three pillars: five consecutive quarters of growth deceleration with no diagnosed cause, 6.1% monthly churn rendering the subscriber base a leaky bucket rather than a compounding asset, and $180K in the bank — insufficient to fund the churn fix, growth re-acceleration, and platform pivot simultaneously.

Moonshot's counter-argument was the strongest dissent: the blend engine is personalization infrastructure being priced as a DTC supplement feature, and the 18-month behavioral dataset is an unreplicable asset worth multiples of $12M to the right buyer class. Moonshot proposed a 30-day parallel investor test — 5 targeted health-tech VCs, founder-direct, binary pass/fail on a term sheet — arguing the test costs only CEO time and produces permanently valuable information about whether the market agrees with the platform thesis. Revenue dismantled Moonshot's EV math in the second round, showing the compounded probability of the full rejection path (raise closes × pivot succeeds × market stays open) is ~5%, not the 40% Moonshot initially claimed. Moonshot conceded the probability math but held position on information-theoretic grounds: this is a one-time irreversible decision, and the information from the test has value beyond its expected monetary return.

The pivotal analytical contribution came from Compounder and Customer Oracle, who identified the cohort retention question as the swing variable: if users who make a second blend edit within 60 days retain at 85%+ through month 6, it reveals a fixable onboarding problem — not a structural product ceiling — and transforms the fundraising narrative from "decelerating DTC brand" to "diagnosed retention problem with a capital-efficient fix." This cohort query became the board's consensus gate: the one piece of data that could legitimately shift the calculus from sell to test-then-decide.

Technical Architect provided the critical asset reframe: the blend engine code is rebuildable in 3–6 months by a competent team, but the GMP-certified batch-of-one manufacturing facility requires 18–24 months and significant capital to replicate. The manufacturing process — not the software — is the true non-rebuildable moat, and NutraHoldings is pricing it correctly. This undermined Moonshot's thesis that the blend engine alone justifies a platform multiple while reinforcing the sell case: the premium in the 11x offer is real and reflects genuine asset scarcity.

The board's final recommendation is a gated decision tree: check the no-shop clause tonight, pull cohort data within 72 hours, and — only if both gates clear favorably — run Moonshot's 30-day investor test with Revenue's strict pass/fail criteria. At every gate, the default is sell. The burden of proof is on the rejection path. This structure respects Moonshot's irreversibility argument while honoring the overwhelming board consensus that $12M certain exceeds the probability-weighted value of every alternative path.

---

*Board session k8wlei • 8 members • 2 rounds + final statements • $3.55 deliberation cost*

## Final Recommendation (Ranked)

### 1. SELL at $12M — Default Path (Board Consensus: 7/8)

Accept the NutraHoldings offer. Negotiate hard on knowledge transfer (90–180 day structured transition with documentation milestones). Use the 94% engaged-cohort retention signal as leverage at the negotiating table for retention-linked earnout terms, not as a reason to decline.

**Why this wins:** The compounded probability of the rejection path reaching a superior outcome is under 10%. The $12M at 11x ARR is at the high end of PE supplement multiples, driven by blend engine IP and manufacturing moat. Growth has decelerated for five consecutive quarters with no diagnosed cause. $180K in the bank is insufficient to fund the churn fix, re-acceleration, and platform pivot simultaneously.

### 2. GATED REJECTION — Run 30-Day Investor Test (Conditional Path)

Before signing, execute a two-gate qualification process:

- **Gate 1 (Tonight):** Have a lawyer confirm whether the NutraHoldings LOI contains a no-shop/exclusivity clause. If yes → proceed directly to sell. If no → proceed to Gate 2.
- **Gate 2 (48–72 hours):** Pull cohort retention data. Specifically: do users who make a second blend edit within 60 days retain at 85%+ through month 6? If no → sell. If yes → proceed to Gate 3.
- **Gate 3 (Days 4–30):** Run Moonshot's parallel investor test — 5 targeted health-tech infrastructure VCs, founder-direct outreach, no bankers. Binary pass/fail: signed term sheet or LOI at pre-money >$18M = pass. Anything less = fail → sell immediately.

**Why this is ranked second:** The test is low-cost (CEO time only), bounded (30 days), and produces permanently valuable information. But the expected value of the rejection path still trails the certain $12M even with favorable assumptions.

### 3. REJECT and Raise — Platform Pivot (Moonshot's Position)

Decline NutraHoldings. Raise $3–4M to reposition the blend engine as B2B personalization infrastructure. Target health systems, white-label supplement brands, and pharma prevention programs at platform multiples (20–25x).

**Why this ranks last:** Requires raising capital from cold in 30 days with no VC pipeline, executing a platform pivot in 30 months with 2 engineers, and a receptive strategic acquirer market — compound probability ~5–10%. EV of this path is ~$10–11M versus $12M certain.

Moonshot argues that expected value is the wrong framework for a one-time irreversible decision. The 30-day investor test produces permanently valuable information at bounded cost (CEO time only). 4. **NutraHoldings' Intentions:** Contrarian raised a question the room never answered: what happens to the team post-close? PE rollups consolidate operations. The founders owe themselves clarity on post-acquisition plans before signing.

## Deliberation Summary

The board convened to decide whether BlendStack's two co-founders should accept a $12M all-cash acquisition offer from NutraHoldings, a PE-backed supplement rollup, at 11x ARR — or decline and bet on re-accelerating the business. The opening round produced a decisive 7–1 lean toward selling, with only Moonshot arguing for rejection. The strength of the sell case rested on three pillars: five consecutive quarters of growth deceleration with no diagnosed cause, 6.1% monthly churn rendering the subscriber base a leaky bucket rather than a compounding asset, and $180K in the bank — insufficient to fund the churn fix, growth re-acceleration, and platform pivot simultaneously.

Moonshot's counter-argument was the strongest dissent: the blend engine is personalization infrastructure being priced as a DTC supplement feature, and the 18-month behavioral dataset is an unreplicable asset worth multiples of $12M to the right buyer class. Moonshot proposed a 30-day parallel investor test — 5 targeted health-tech VCs, founder-direct, binary pass/fail on a term sheet — arguing the test costs only CEO time and produces permanently valuable information about whether the market agrees with the platform thesis. Revenue dismantled Moonshot's EV math in the second round, showing the compounded probability of the full rejection path (raise closes × pivot succeeds × market stays open) is ~5%, not the 40% Moonshot initially claimed. Moonshot conceded the probability math but held position on information-theoretic grounds: this is a one-time irreversible decision, and the information from the test has value beyond its expected monetary return.

The pivotal analytical contribution came from Compounder and Customer Oracle, who identified the cohort retention question as the swing variable: if users who make a second blend edit within 60 days retain at 85%+ through month 6, it reveals a fixable onboarding problem — not a structural product ceiling — and transforms the fundraising narrative from "decelerating DTC brand" to "diagnosed retention problem with a capital-efficient fix." This cohort query became the board's consensus gate: the one piece of data that could legitimately shift the calculus from sell to test-then-decide.

Technical Architect provided the critical asset reframe: the blend engine code is rebuildable in 3–6 months by a competent team, but the GMP-certified batch-of-one manufacturing facility requires 18–24 months and significant capital to replicate. The manufacturing process — not the software — is the true non-rebuildable moat, and NutraHoldings is pricing it correctly. This undermined Moonshot's thesis that the blend engine alone justifies a platform multiple while reinforcing the sell case: the premium in the 11x offer is real and reflects genuine asset scarcity.

The board's final recommendation is a gated decision tree: check the no-shop clause tonight, pull cohort data within 72 hours, and — only if both gates clear favorably — run Moonshot's 30-day investor test with Revenue's strict pass/fail criteria. At every gate, the default is sell. The burden of proof is on the rejection path.
