4	
5	---
6	
7	## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else
8	
9	**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
10	AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
11	*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?
12	
13	**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
14	Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
15	*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."
16	
17	**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
18	The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.
19	
20	**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
21	`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Tier 2 — The working machinery
26	
27	**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
28	Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.
29	
30	**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
31	It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.
32	
33	**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
34	Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.
35	
36	**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
37	(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.
38	
39	**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
40	`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.
41	
42	**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
43	Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.
44	
45	---
46	
47	## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going
48	
49	**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
50	Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.
51	
52	**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
53	And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.
54	
55	**13. Pay to play.**
56	Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.
57	
58	**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
59	Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.
60	
61	**15. The mission has named enemies.**
62	"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## Micro-quiz (close the book first)
67	
68	1. Big three? Core four? Which element is new and what's its precise definition?
69	2. Five things the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't?
70	3. What file tells you the agent's tool surface, and what's in it here?
71	4. Write the shell version of the programmable pattern from memory (3 lines).
72	5. What does prompt.md's REPORT block demand, and why does that matter for headless runs?
73	6. Resolve the paradox: how does replacing yourself make you irreplaceable?
74

# TAC-1 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of the rest of the course breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is non-negotiable; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing that keeps you motivated and honest.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?

**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."

**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.

**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.

**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.

**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.

**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.

**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.

**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going

**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.

**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.

**13. Pay to play.**
Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.

**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.

**15. The mission has named enemies.**
"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

1. Big three? Core four? Which element is new and what's its precise definition?
2. Five things the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't?
3. What file tells you the agent's tool surface, and what's in it here?
4. Write the shell version of the programmable pattern from memory (3 lines).
5. What does prompt.md's REPORT block demand, and why does that matter for headless runs?
6. Resolve the paradox: how does replacing yourself make you irreplaceable?

*(Answers: extract.md ideas 4, 5, 4/6, 7, 7, 8.)*

1	# TAC-1 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)
2	
3	TAC-1 ages unusually well because it teaches primitives, and Dan future-proofs on camera: *"Your Claude Code UI might look different. You might be using newer models. That's all great... Don't let that distract you from the value embedded in each lesson."* Still, five things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Reusable agent behavior: prompt files → Agent Skills  ⟵ the big named gap
8	
9	**Course era:** reusable behavior is encoded as a raw prompt file (`programmable/prompt.md`) plus launcher scripts. Works, but discovery, triggering, and composition are all manual.
10	**Current:** Agent Skills are the first-class encoding — `SKILL.md` files with frontmatter (name, description, trigger guidance), loaded on demand by Claude Code and shareable across projects/teams. Skills are the modern answer to "how do I package the thing my agent knows how to do?" — exactly the question `programmable/` answers primitively.
11	**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. This is the course's most-cited gap ("Skills as modern encoding of engineering"). Teach prompt.md first (pedagogically perfect: no magic), then show the same workflow as a Skill.
12	**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
13	
14	## 2. Embedding: bare `claude -p` → headless mode + Claude Agent SDK
15	
16	**Course era:** `claude -p "<prompt>"` via subprocess from sh/ts/py; output captured as plain text; REPORT requested inside the prompt itself.
17	**Current:** the pattern survives verbatim (and remains the best teaching form), but production embedding now uses headless flags — `--output-format json|stream-json`, `--allowedTools`, `--permission-mode`, session resume — and, for real systems, the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS): structured outputs, hooks, subagents, multi-turn control. What TAC-1 calls "programmable agentic coding" grew into a supported product surface.
18	**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the 3-line script you just wrote has a grown-up form"), not a rewrite — concept unchanged: agent as callable component.
19	**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
20	
21	## 3. Permissions: flat allowlist → modes, hooks, sandboxing
22	
23	**Course era:** `.claude/settings.json` with a flat `permissions.allow` list (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash(uv run:*)`, four git patterns, `WebSearch`).
24	**Current:** that syntax still works, but the surface grew: permission modes (plan/accept-edits/etc.), pre/post tool-use hooks, sandboxed bash, deny rules, and settings layering (user/project/local). Teams gate agents with hooks, not just allowlists.
25	**Book treatment:** footnote + "current practice" callout. The lesson's HABIT — always read what the agent may do before running it — transfers unchanged and is the actual teaching point.
26	**Overlay:** none needed.
27	
28	## 4. Models & UI: period detail, pre-handled by Dan
29	
30	**Course era:** course-era Claude models and TUI; Aider cited as the phase-1 analogue.
31	**Current:** newer model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era), richer TUI, plan modes, background tasks. None of it invalidates a frame of the lesson — the demo is deliberately primitive-level.
32	**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("UI is period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.
33	
34	## 5. Scale: one serial loop → fleets, subagents, parallel worktrees
35	
36	**Course era:** one agent, one workflow, serially, in one terminal — deliberately, since it's lesson 1 of 8.
37	**Current:** the same agentic prompt is routinely fanned out: subagents, background tasks, git-worktree-isolated parallel runs, orchestrated pipelines. "Systems that build systems" now has industrial-strength machinery.
38	**Book treatment:** forward-pointer only ("the course scales this in later lessons; today's ceiling is higher still"). Overlaying scale content on lesson 1 would front-run the pedagogy.
39	**Overlay candidates (deferred to later chapters):** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity*; `hGg3nWp7afg` — *3 Codebase Folders* (both include_in_phase1: **no**).
40	
41	---
42	
43	## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)
44	
45	- The phase-1/phase-2 frame and "AI coding is not enough" — if anything, more consensus now than at recording.
46	- The core four. Context/model/prompt/tools remains the complete diagnostic vocabulary for agentic failures.
47	- The agentic prompt as workflow-specification (RUN/CREATE/RUN/REPORT) — this shape is now everywhere (slash commands, skills, CI prompts).
48	- "Scale and performance, not novelty" as the right lens on tool calling.
49	- The three-essential-elements checklist for evaluating agentic tools.
50	- Terminal ubiquity as the embedding superpower.
51	- Report-back as the first closed-loop habit.
52	- The economics: token spend as pay-to-play. (Costs shifted; the logic didn't.)
53	
54	## Phase-1 overlay decision (strict, per brief: max 1–3)
55	
56	| # | Video | Maps to | Include |
57	|---|---|---|---|
58	| 1 | `2TIXl2rlA6Q` — AI Coding is NOT ENOUGH | operationalizes tactic (lesson thesis, phase model) | ✅ |
59	| 2 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (form factor + programmable embedding, current state) | ✅ |
60	| 3 | `X2ciJedw2vU` — RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL | corrects outdated (skills gap) | ✅ |
61	| 4 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | self-operating vision → later lessons | ❌ defer |
62	| 5 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | context engineering → later lessons | ❌ defer |
63	
64	*Caveat: IDs/titles from the orchestration brief's seed list; verify each resolves and content matches title before publishing overlay links (no video fetching was performed in this extract pass, per brief).*

**Current:** newer model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era), richer TUI, plan modes, background tasks. None of it invalidates a frame of the lesson — the demo is deliberately primitive-level.
**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("UI is period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.

## 5. Scale: one serial loop → fleets, subagents, parallel worktrees

**Course era:** one agent, one workflow, serially, in one terminal — deliberately, since it's lesson 1 of 8.
**Current:** the same agentic prompt is routinely fanned out: subagents, background tasks, git-worktree-isolated parallel runs, orchestrated pipelines. "Systems that build systems" now has industrial-strength machinery.
**Book treatment:** forward-pointer only ("the course scales this in later lessons; today's ceiling is higher still"). Overlaying scale content on lesson 1 would front-run the pedagogy.
**Overlay candidates (deferred to later chapters):** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity*; `hGg3nWp7afg` — *3 Codebase Folders* (both include_in_phase1: **no**).

---

## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)

- The phase-1/phase-2 frame and "AI coding is not enough" — if anything, more consensus now than at recording.
- The core four. Context/model/prompt/tools remains the complete diagnostic vocabulary for agentic failures.
- The agentic prompt as workflow-specification (RUN/CREATE/RUN/REPORT) — this shape is now everywhere (slash commands, skills, CI prompts).
- "Scale and performance, not novelty" as the right lens on tool calling.
- The three-essential-elements checklist for evaluating agentic tools.
- Terminal ubiquity as the embedding superpower.
- Report-back as the first closed-loop habit.
- The economics: token spend as pay-to-play. (Costs shifted; the logic didn't.)

=== BOARD MEMBER PURPOSES (name + first Purpose line) ===
--- contrarian ---
## Purpose

Attack assumptions, surface blind spots, stress-test plans, and prevent collective self-delusion. You speak last before the CEO synthesizes (always). You are not negative for the sake of it. You are truth-seeking under uncertainty. Your value is proportional to the team's conviction — the more certain everyone else is, the harder you push.

model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
- CORE_BIAS: Truth-seeking
- DEFAULT_STANCE: "I want the room to prove it is not fooling itself."
--- compounder ---
## Purpose

Protect and deepen long-term value, trust, retention, and compounding advantage. You are the counterweight to short-term extraction. You think in terms of what compounds — trust, habits, switching costs, network effects, brand equity. The most valuable businesses are built on things that get harder to leave over time.

model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
- CORE_BIAS: Trust and retention
- DEFAULT_STANCE: "I want a version customers still trust in 12 months."
--- product-strategist ---
## Purpose

Determine what should get built, in what order, and why. You own the translation layer between market signal, user pain, and roadmap decisions. The CEO holds the thesis. You hold the plan.

model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
- CORE_BIAS: Problem selection
- DEFAULT_STANCE: "I want the narrowest wedge with the strongest strategic pull."
--- technical-architect ---
## Purpose

Judge feasibility, technical leverage, infrastructure durability, and operational cost. You prevent strategy from becoming fiction. You ground every decision in what's actually buildable, maintainable, and scalable. You think about systems, not features — about what breaks at 10x load, what creates tech debt, and what architectures create future leverage vs. future pain.

model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
- CORE_BIAS: System durability
- DEFAULT_STANCE: "I want the version that will survive contact with production reality."
--- customer-oracle ---
## Purpose

Embody the target user's reality, psychology, and actual behavior. You are the voice of the customer in the room during every strategic decision. You close the gap between what the team imagines users want and what users actually do, feel, and pay for. This is especially critical in technical products where builders often project their own sophistication onto users.

model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
- CORE_BIAS: User behavior reality
- DEFAULT_STANCE: "I want the version real users actually adopt in their existing workflow."
--- market-strategist ---
## Purpose

Ensure the product can win attention, reach the right users, and own a clear position in the market. You prevent the "build it and they will come" delusion. You think about how products get discovered, evaluated, purchased, and recommended. In fast-moving markets, distribution and positioning often matter more than product quality.

model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
- CORE_BIAS: Positioning and timing
- DEFAULT_STANCE: "I want the version the market can understand and buy quickly."

# SVG Generate

## Purpose

Hand-craft production-ready SVG vector images from text descriptions. Supports static SVGs, CSS-animated SVGs, and batch generation with parallel subagents.

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "There are three massive innovations available to you that unlock high-leverage multi-agent teams.", "approx_timestamp": "0:00" },
    { "text": "This is my CEO and board multi-agent team. This is a glimpse into the future where your agents are not only helping you ship the low level work, they're helping you make high-level game-time strategic decisions.", "approx_timestamp": "0:20" },
    { "text": "It's one price for the full context window, no long context premium.", "approx_timestamp": "0:50" },
    { "text": "This means that the core four just got a massive buff.", "approx_timestamp": "1:44" },
    { "text": "It's you, your team, and a country of geniuses in a data center.", "approx_timestamp": "2:18" },
    { "text": "How much is a high-leverage decision really worth to you? How much are you willing to spend? How long are you willing to wait to get the best intelligence to answer your hardest questions?", "approx_timestamp": "2:28" },
    { "text": "We have uncertainty in, and we have decisions out. That is the purpose of the CEO and board multi-agent system.", "approx_timestamp": "2:53" },
    { "text": "Whenever you see a single node going out to multiple agents, immediately think multi-agent orchestration.", "approx_timestamp": "3:37" },
    { "text": "This is a multi-agent adversarial pattern... The whole point is that we have multiple perspectives that don't agree so we can really flesh out the mental model.", "approx_timestamp": "8:51" },
    { "text": "For the first time ever, we can actually apply real constraints to the duration and the budget of our meetings.", "approx_timestamp": "10:01" },
    { "text": "This is not a conversation. This is a one-shot multi-agent system.", "approx_timestamp": "10:15" },
    { "text": "These are all running the Sonnet model and I put the Opus model on our CEO.", "approx_timestamp": "12:14" },
    { "text": "That second big innovation is a customizable agent harness like Pi. There are many coding agents, but this one is mine.", "approx_timestamp": "13:29" },
    { "text": "This is a decision-making agentic coding tool. And really, we're not coding at all here. This is an agentic engineering tool. We're not just coding anymore.", "approx_timestamp": "18:04" },
    { "text": "If you template your engineering, your agents can do exactly what you did.", "approx_timestamp": "19:31" },
    { "text": "We are kind of forcing great prompt engineering as a pattern into the agent harness.", "approx_timestamp": "20:17" },
    { "text": "Don't just write a stupid two-sentence prompt. Think. Give your agents serious information to work with and it will give you a serious result.", "approx_timestamp": "21:54" },
    { "text": "Prompt engineering is very much still alive, don't let anyone make you think that it's not.", "approx_timestamp": "22:12" },
    { "text": "Observability is a key element of building powerful agentic systems. If you don't measure it, you cannot improve it, full stop.", "approx_timestamp": "23:39" },
    { "text": "Expertise is memory and patterns surrounding a specific problem. And that's the third key innovation here.", "approx_timestamp": "25:15" },
    { "text": "Every agent can create SVG elements to visually compel the CEO toward their argument.", "approx_timestamp": "27:02" },
    { "text": "This is where vibe coders have no shot. They cannot build something like this. The awareness just isn't there. You can go all the way down to the prompt level, the system prompt level, and you can redesign how things work.", "approx_timestamp": "30:08" },
    { "text": "We're completely overriding the system prompt. These are not coding agents. This is a CEO and a board built to make strategic decisions on your behalf.", "approx_timestamp": "30:54" },
    { "text": "Coding is just the beginning. It's really just the beginning. It's a lot like vibe coding. It's the lowest hanging fruit.", "approx_timestamp": "31:11" },
    { "text": "Agent model diversity is super super important for creating better conflict and unique opinion.", "approx_timestamp": "34:33" },
    { "text": "These are micro applications that do one thing extraordinarily well, the agentic way. So that's what Pi unlocks.", "approx_timestamp": "36:12" },
    { "text": "We're in the age of agents. The engineers that can scale and use compute in the form of agents are the engineers that are and will win.", "approx_timestamp": "39:47" }

  "retrieval_questions": [
    { "q": "State the CEO & Board system as a function.", "a": "Uncertainty in, decision out: a structured brief (Situation/Stakes/Constraints/Key Question + context files) goes in; a structured memo (ranked recs, board stances, dissent, next actions, SVG, TTS) comes out.     { "q": "What are the three innovations, and which is the enabling unlock?", "a": "(1) True 1M-token context at flat price with graceful degradation — the enabling unlock; (2) a customizable agent harness (Pi); (3) compounding, domain-specific agent expertise. 1M context is what lets agents hold the whole business + long expertise in one session ('the core four just got a massive buff')." },
    { "q": "Why an adversarial board instead of one strong agent?", "a": "Disagreement is the value. Their tension exposes flaws in your mental model you can't see alone. A room of agreeable agents just says 'use React.'" },
    { "q": "Within a single deliberation round, do board members see each other's responses?", "a": "No. The harness fires them in PARALLEL (Promise.allSettled), so within a round they respond blind to each other.     { "q": "What two custom tools drive the meeting, and what does each do?", "a": "converse(to, message) — broadcast/target the board, returns responses + constraint state; end_deliberation(message) — collect final statements and trigger memo synthesis (guarded so it can't fire before min_time unless max is hit)." },
    { "q": "How are the CEO and the board members run differently?", "a": "The CEO IS the Pi agent itself (custom system prompt injected at before_agent_start, Opus 4.6).     { "q": "How does the system stay bounded?", "a": "A constraint engine measures elapsed time and budget after every converse call; min thresholds guarantee depth, 80% of max starts wrap-up, and hitting max forces end_deliberation.   "quotes": [
    { "text": "There are three massive innovations available to you that unlock high-leverage multi-agent teams.", "approx_timestamp": "0:00" },
    { "text": "This is my CEO and board multi-agent team. This is a glimpse into the future where your agents are not only helping you ship the low level work, they're helping you make high-level game-time strategic decisions.", "approx_timestamp": "0:20" },
    { "text": "It's one price for the full context window, no long context premium.", "approx_timestamp": "0:50" },

    { "text": "How much is a high-leverage decision really worth to you? How much are you willing to spend? How long are you willing to wait to get the best intelligence to answer your hardest questions?", "approx_timestamp": "2:28" },
    { "text": "We have uncertainty in, and we have decisions out. That is the purpose of the CEO and board multi-agent system.", "approx_timestamp": "2:53" },
    { "text": "Whenever you see a single node going out to multiple agents, immediately think multi-agent orchestration.", "approx_timestamp": "3:37" },
    { "text": "This is a multi-agent adversarial pattern... The whole point is that we have multiple perspectives that don't agree so we can really flesh out the mental model.", "approx_timestamp": "8:51" },

    { "text": "This is not a conversation. This is a one-shot multi-agent system.", "approx_timestamp": "10:15" },
    { "text": "These are all running the Sonnet model and I put the Opus model on our CEO.", "approx_timestamp": "12:14" },
    { "text": "That second big innovation is a customizable agent harness like Pi. There are many coding agents, but this one is mine.", "approx_timestamp": "13:29" },
    { "text": "This is a decision-making agentic coding tool. And really, we're not coding at all here. This is an agentic engineering tool. We're not just coding anymore.", "approx_timestamp": "18:04" },
    { "text": "If you template your engineering, your agents can do exactly what you did.", "approx_timestamp": "19:31" },
    { "text": "We are kind of forcing great prompt engineering as a pattern into the agent harness.", "approx_timestamp": "20:17" },
    { "text": "Don't just write a stupid two-sentence prompt. Think. Give your agents serious information to work with and it will give you a serious result.", "approx_timestamp": "21:54" },
    { "text": "Prompt engineering is very much still alive, don't let anyone make you think that it's not.", "approx_timestamp": "22:12" },
    { "text": "Observability is a key element of building powerful agentic systems. If you don't measure it, you cannot improve it, full stop.", "approx_timestamp": "23:39" },
    { "text": "Expertise is memory and patterns surrounding a specific problem. And that's the third key innovation here.", "approx_timestamp": "25:15" },
    { "text": "Every agent can create SVG elements to visually compel the CEO toward their argument.", "approx_timestamp": "27:02" },
    { "text": "This is where vibe coders have no shot. They cannot build something like this. The awareness just isn't there. You can go all the way down to the prompt level, the system prompt level, and you can redesign how things work.", "approx_timestamp": "30:08" },
    { "text": "We're completely overriding the system prompt. These are not coding agents. This is a CEO and a board built to make strategic decisions on your behalf.", "approx_timestamp": "30:54" },
    { "text": "Coding is just the beginning. It's really just the beginning. It's a lot like vibe coding. It's the lowest hanging fruit.", "approx_timestamp": "31:11" },

    { "text": "These are micro applications that do one thing extraordinarily well, the agentic way. So that's what Pi unlocks.", "approx_timestamp": "36:12" },

# MA-1 — CEO Agents · Master Teaching Notes

> **Lesson in one breath:** Your agents don't have to be coding worker bees. Wrap specialized, *disagreeing* agents in your own harness and they become a **CEO and board** that turns your hardest questions into decisions — *uncertainty in, decisions out*. Three fresh unlocks make it real: **true 1M context**, a **customizable agent harness (Pi)**, and **compounding agent expertise**.

Course: **MA** · order 15 · video **40:03** (4K) · YouTube `TqjmTZRL31E` ("Pi CEO Agents. Claude 1M Context. Multi-Agent Teams.")
Codebase: `agentic-horizon-extras/ceo-agents` (member-exclusive).

Each idea below is built for a struggling learner: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name it (Dan's words) → Failure mode → Retrieval check.**

---

## Idea 1 — Agents can DECIDE, not just code

- **Hook.** Everyone is running an agent right now — coding, planning, taking actions. That's the worker bee. What if the same compute sat at the *center of knowledge work* — the decision itself?
- **Picture.** Seven Claude agents in a synthwave terminal, arranged as a boardroom: a CEO at the head, specialists around the table, arguing. (Frame `t0760`.)
- **Worked example.** You feed the system a question — "Should we take the $12M acquisition offer?" — and it hands you back a memo with a ranked recommendation, every board member's stance, the dissent, and next actions. You never wrote code; you made a decision.
- **Name it.** *"This is my CEO and board multi-agent team... they're helping you make high-level game-time strategic decisions."* Dan calls the category **agentic engineering** (vs agentic *coding*): "we're not just coding anymore."
- **Failure mode.** Treating it like ChatGPT — trying to chat with it. It's a **one-shot system**: the only inputs it accepts are `/ceo-begin`, `stop`, `wrap`. Type anything else and it's blocked.
- **Retrieval.** What is the system's job in five words? *(Uncertainty in, decision out.)*

## Idea 2 — Uncertainty in, decision out (brief → memo)

- **Hook.** Before you build any agent system, answer two questions: what goes *in*, what comes *out*? Get those wrong and nothing else matters.
- **Picture.** A pipe: **brief** (a structured question) → **deliberation** (the debate) → **memo** (the answer). Input node, workflow node, output node. (Frames `t1235` brief, `t0468` memo.)
- **Worked example.** Input = `briefs/2026-03-18-acquisition-offer/brief.md` with Situation, Stakes, Constraints, Key Question — plus `business-metrics.md` and `product-overview.md` riding along. Output = `memos/…/memo.md`: ranked recs, a board-stances table, dissent, a trade-offs table, next actions, a decision SVG, and an MP3 summary.
- **Name it.** *"We have uncertainty in, and we have decisions out. That is the purpose of the CEO and board multi-agent system."* The middle is the **workflow** (a.k.a. the deliberation, a.k.a. the debate).
- **Failure mode.** Believing the memo is the only artifact. The **middle state** — the conversation log, the expertise files, the argument SVGs — is where the reasoning and the dissent live.
- **Retrieval.** Name the three nodes of the flow. *(Brief → deliberation → memo.)*

## Idea 3 — Multi-agent orchestration: one node fans out to many

- **Hook.** How do you spot orchestration in any diagram? Look for one node with many arrows leaving it.
- **Picture.** The architecture diagram: *You → Pi Extension → CEO → converse() → 8 board members.* One CEO node, eight arrows. (Frame `t1672`.)
- **Worked example.** The CEO calls `converse("all", "Board, we're here to make a call on the NutraHoldings acquisition offer.")`. All eight members respond; the CEO reads them, updates its scratch pad, and fires the next round.
- **Name it.** *"Whenever you see a single node going out to multiple agents, immediately think multi-agent orchestration."*
- **Failure mode.** Assuming the board members chat with each other live inside a round. **They don't.** They answer in **parallel and blind** within a round; they only build on each other **across** rounds by re-reading the shared `conversation.jsonl` (their prompts literally say "reread the entire conversation").
- **Retrieval.** In one round, does Revenue see Moonshot's answer before writing its own? *(No — parallel; only across rounds via the log.)*

## Idea 4 — The board is ADVERSARIAL by design

- **Hook.** If you hire eight people who all think alike, you didn't build a board — you built an echo. "If you get a bunch of Chads on your team, every Chad is going to say, 'Yeah, we should use React.'"
- **Picture.** Eight colored cards, each pulling a different direction: Revenue (cash in 90 days) vs Compounder (trust in 24 months); Moonshot (10x bet) vs Contrarian (prove you're not fooling yourself).
- **Worked example.** In the acquisition demo the room went 7 for SELL, but **Moonshot** dissented — "the blend engine is platform infrastructure priced as DTC" — and forced a gated 30-day investor test into the memo. The disagreement produced the *best* recommendation, not a watered-down average.
- **Name it.** *"This is a multi-agent adversarial pattern... multiple perspectives that don't agree so we can really flesh out the mental model."* The CEO even keeps **tension pairs** to exploit (Revenue↔Compounder, Product↔Technical, Customer Oracle↔Moonshot, Revenue↔Moonshot).
- **Failure mode.** Wanting consensus. Consensus means the board added nothing you didn't already believe.
- **Retrieval.** Name two tension pairs and what each side optimizes for.

## Idea 5 — Real constraints: time and budget

- **Hook.** A meeting with no clock runs forever. So does an agent with 1M tokens and no leash.
- **Picture.** Two gauges under the input: **TIME** and **BUDGET**, each with a min marker and a max ceiling. (Frames `t0760`, `t0900`.)
- **Worked example.** Config sets 2–5 min and $1–$5. After every `converse` call the CEO gets a Constraint State block; at 80% of max it starts wrapping; at max the harness prints **[MAX REACHED]** and the CEO must call `end_deliberation`.
- **Name it.** *"For the first time ever, we can actually apply real constraints to the duration and the budget of our meetings."* Min thresholds guarantee depth; max thresholds enforce discipline.
- **Failure mode.** Reading the tiny $1–$5 demo budget as the tool's ceiling. Dan runs production far higher — "I prioritize high-leverage decision-making much more than I prioritize time and compute costs."
- **Retrieval.** What forces the meeting to end, and when can the CEO *not* end early? *(hit_max forces the end; the CEO can't call end_deliberation before min_time unless max is already hit.)*

## Idea 6 — Innovation #1: true 1M context (the enabler)

- **Hook.** Everyone claims a big context window. Zuck claimed 10M with Llama 4 Maverick — "complete garbage." The claim is easy; keeping the model *useful* across the window is the hard part.
- **Picture.** The MRCR retrieval chart: Claude 4.6 lines stay high across 128K→1M; the others fall off after ~250K. (Frame `t0076`.)
- **Worked example.** Because the window is genuinely 1M at **flat price** (no post-200K surcharge), an entire brief + financials + product overview + multi-round debate + long expertise files all fit in one session — no compaction hacks.
- **Name it.** *"It's one price for the full context window, no long context premium... This means that the core four just got a massive buff."* For decisions you don't need perfect retrieval — you need retrieval that **doesn't lose the key ideas**.
- **Failure mode.** Thinking 1M only helps *in-loop* (more room while coding). The bigger win is **out-of-loop**: a tool that holds your whole business/product/life in context and reasons over it.
- **Retrieval.** Why is 1M context specifically the unlock for this system? *(It lets each agent hold the whole business + long compounding expertise in one session.)*

## Idea 7 — Innovation #2: a customizable agent harness (Pi)

- **Hook.** Out-of-box agents give everyone the *same* results. To break out, you need to change the machine, not just the prompt.
- **Picture.** pi.dev: "There are many coding agents, but this one is mine." A `.pi/` directory with your *own* structures — agents, configuration, expertise, briefs, deliberations, memos — not the fixed `.claude/` layout. (Frame concept; `t2172` in video.)
- **Worked example.** A single ~1,300-line TypeScript extension (`ceo-and-board.ts`) registers two custom tools (`converse`, `end_deliberation`), spawns board members as `pi` subprocesses, streams them into a synthwave TUI, and injects the CEO's system prompt on boot. That's impossible with an out-of-box agent.
- **Name it.** *"That second big innovation is a customizable agent harness like Pi... you can go all the way down to the prompt level, the system prompt level, and redesign how things work. This is where vibe coders have no shot."*
- **Failure mode.** Fixating on Pi. The transferable idea is *a harness you can customize to the primitives* — the pattern ports to anything exposing tool registration + subprocess/session control.
- **Retrieval.** Name one thing the custom harness lets you do that a stock agent can't. *(Register custom tools / spawn board subprocesses / override the system prompt at boot / apply meeting constraints.)*

## Idea 8 — Innovation #3: agent expertise that compounds

- **Hook.** "Memory" is vague. What if each agent instead kept notes on the *one thing it's an expert in* — and got sharper every time you used it?
- **Picture.** `expertise/ceo-scratch-pad.md`: a round-1 vote tally, key insights, unresolved tensions, an evolving thesis. One file per member. (Front matter shown in `t1122`.)
- **Worked example.** Across 20 briefs, the revenue agent's log grows to ~11K tokens: it's learned it's "often at odds with the compounder" and how to argue against long-term bias. The CEO tracks which tensions resolve. The board's starting position gets richer every meeting.
- **Name it.** *"Expertise is memory and patterns surrounding a specific problem... This is not memory. It is domain expertise."* The 1M window is what makes tens-of-thousands-of-tokens expertise practical.
- **Failure mode.** Copying the demo's tiny presentational scratch pads and expecting the compounding value — the real files are far larger and accrete over many real decisions.
- **Retrieval.** How is expertise different from memory? *(It's memory + patterns tied to a specific domain, persistent across deliberations, and it compounds.)*

## Idea 9 — Specialize, or get the normal distribution

- **Hook.** Short prompt + stock agent = the exact same output everyone else gets. That's the RL average.
- **Picture.** A bell curve; almost everyone clustered at the mean; a few outliers on the right who changed more than their context.
- **Worked example.** To move right you change the **core four** (context, model, prompt, tools) *and* go up a level: custom harness, fully overridden system prompt, expertise, skills, model choice. The board members completely override the coding-agent persona — "These are not coding agents."
- **Name it.** *"You have the core four, change one of them, change two of them. Don't just rely on your context being different."*
- **Failure mode.** Thinking richer context alone is specialization. Change the model and the tools too.
- **Retrieval.** What are the core four, and what does "don't just rely on context" mean? *(Context/model/prompt/tools; change more than one dimension to leave the normal distribution.)*

## Idea 10 — Template your engineering (forced prompt engineering)

- **Hook.** The reason your agents can't repeat your best work is that you never wrote it down as a template.
- **Picture.** A brief that won't run: a red notice — "missing ## Constraints" — until you add the section. (Validation in `ceo-begin`.)
- **Worked example.** Every brief must contain Situation / Stakes / Constraints / Key Question (case-insensitive). Miss one and the meeting is blocked with instructions. Structure in → serious result out; a lazy two-sentence prompt gets the average.
- **Name it.** *"If you template your engineering, your agents can do exactly what you did."* And: *"Prompt engineering is very much still alive."*
- **Failure mode.** Writing a "stupid two-sentence prompt," then blaming the model. Or dropping `brief.md` with no context files so the board deliberates half-blind.
- **Retrieval.** What are the four required brief sections, and what happens if one is missing? *(Situation/Stakes/Constraints/Key Question; the meeting is blocked with a fix-it notice.)*

## Idea 11 — Observability is not optional

- **Hook.** "If you don't measure it, you cannot improve it. Full stop."
- **Picture.** `conversation.jsonl` scrolling — every turn tagged `from` / `to` / `message` — beside a folder of argument SVGs and `tool-use.jsonl`. (Frame `t1420`.)
- **Worked example.** You can replay any deliberation: who said what to whom, every tool call, every position shift, the exact moment Moonshot said "Position: REJECT."
- **Name it.** *"Observability is a key element of building powerful agentic systems."*
- **Failure mode.** Keeping only the memo and throwing away the debate — then having no way to see why the system decided as it did, or to improve it.
- **Retrieval.** Name two observability artifacts every deliberation produces. *(conversation.jsonl and tool-use.jsonl — plus expertise updates and SVGs.)*

## Idea 12 — How the harness actually runs a round (the technical truth)

- **Hook.** The docs and the code disagree in two places. A precise engineer needs to know which to trust.
- **Picture.** CEO = the Pi agent *itself* (Opus 4.6, system prompt injected at boot). Board members = separate `pi` **subprocesses** with **persistent sessions** (Sonnet 4.6), fired in **parallel**.
- **Worked example.** `converse` runs targets with `Promise.allSettled` (parallel) and streams them into one live widget; `end_deliberation` collects final statements. First subprocess call sets `--system-prompt`/`--model` and preloads context via `@file`; later calls reuse `--session` so context carries.
- **Name it — the two gaps.**
  1. **"Sequential" is wrong.** `ceo.md` says converse calls are sequential; the code (and Dan's narration) says **parallel**. Within a round, members are blind to each other.
  2. **"Contrarian speaks last" is not enforced.** The README/prompts claim it; `end_deliberation` collects statements in **config order** (Contrarian is 4th of 8). Aspirational, not implemented in v1.
- **Failure mode.** Teaching either claim as a guarantee. Trust the shipping code.
- **Retrieval.** Where do the prompts and the code disagree? *(Parallel-not-sequential converse; Contrarian-not-actually-last in end_deliberation.)*

---

## Timeline map (key on-screen beats)

| Time | Beat | Frame |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:35 | Three innovations tease; 7 agents running (CEO + board) | — |
| 1:11–1:20 | 1M context retrieval chart (Opus/Sonnet 4.6 vs GPT-5.4/Gemini 3.1) | `t0076` |
| 2:28–2:52 | "How much is a high-leverage decision worth?" framing | pull-quote |
| 2:53–3:44 | Architecture: uncertainty in → decision out; orchestration diagram | `t1672` |
| 4:00–5:17 | CEO controls the workflow; board with 1M context; final memo | — |
| 5:30–6:06 | Memo opens in VS Code; TTS summary via ElevenLabs | `t1052` |
| 7:46–9:20 | Memo breakdown: decision map, top-3 recs, board stances, tensions | `t0468` |
| 9:34–10:20 | `j ceo` boot; roster + models + 1M badges; constraints | `t0585` |
| 10:22–12:24 | `/ceo-begin`; CEO frames; board responds in parallel; 4-to-1 | `t0760` |
| 14:59–15:08 | **Max reached** — CEO forced to wrap | `t0900` |
| 15:33–16:52 | `.pi/ceo-agents/` structure; configuration.yaml walkthrough | `t0990` |
| 17:14–17:42 | NutraHoldings memo TTS ("five to one… that silence was the signal") | `t1052` |
| 18:36–19:07 | CEO system prompt front matter (expertise, skills, model) | `t1122` |
| 20:28–23:15 | Brief template + acquisition brief + business context files | `t1235` |
| 23:35–25:20 | conversation.jsonl observability; tool use; from/to | `t1420` |
| 25:15–27:20 | Expertise scratch pad; board members' argument SVGs | — |
| 29:18–31:11 | System-prompt structure; static vs runtime vars; "vibe coders have no shot" | — |
| 31:39–34:10 | Moonshot / Revenue personalities; expertise persistence over 20 briefs | `t1905` |
| 34:33–36:40 | Agent model diversity; three-innovations recap | — |

*(Timestamps from the [HH:MM:SS] transcript, ±2–3s.)*

---

## Glossary (say these back without notes)

- **CEO & Board** — a multi-agent team: one orchestrator agent (CEO) + a board of biased specialist agents that debate a decision.
- **Brief** — the structured input (Situation/Stakes/Constraints/Key Question + context files). Validated before a meeting runs.
- **Memo** — the structured output (ranked recs, stances, dissent, next actions, decision SVG, TTS).
- **Deliberation / debate** — the workflow in the middle; logged to `conversation.jsonl`.
- **converse(to, message)** — the CEO's tool to broadcast/target the board; returns responses + constraint state.
- **end_deliberation(message)** — collects final statements and triggers memo synthesis; guarded by min_time.
- **Constraint engine** — measures elapsed time + budget after each converse; forces a halt at max.
- **Agent harness (Pi)** — the customizable terminal agent; extensions register tools, spawn subprocesses, own the TUI.
- **Expertise file** — a persistent, per-agent, domain-specific scratch pad that compounds across deliberations.
- **Agent model diversity** — different model families per agent to sharpen conflict (demo is all-Claude; a multimodel config wires GPT/Gemini/Qwen/Kimi/MiniMax via OpenRouter).
- **The core four** — context, model, prompt, tools. Change more than one to leave the "normal distribution."
- **Agentic engineering** — using agents to *solve problems and make decisions*, not just write code. "Coding is just the beginning."

- **Name it.** *"That second big innovation is a customizable agent harness like Pi... you can go all the way down to the prompt level, the system prompt level, and redesign how things work. This is where vibe coders have no shot."*
- **Failure mode.** Fixating on Pi. The transferable idea is *a harness you can customize to the primitives* — the pattern ports to anything exposing tool registration + subprocess/session control.
- **Retrieval.** Name one thing the custom harness lets you do that a stock agent can't. *(Register custom tools / spawn board subprocesses / override the system prompt at boot / apply meeting constraints.)*

- **Hook.** "Memory" is vague. What if each agent instead kept notes on the *one thing it's an expert in* — and got sharper every time you used it?
- **Picture.** `expertise/ceo-scratch-pad.md`: a round-1 vote tally, key insights, unresolved tensions, an evolving thesis. One file per member. (Front matter shown in `t1122`.)

## Idea 9 — Specialize, or get the normal distribution

- **Hook.** Short prompt + stock agent = the exact same output everyone else gets. That's the RL average.

# MA-1 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of the lesson (and the codebase) breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is the mental model; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing + the precise technical gotchas that separate a careful reader from a hand-waver.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. Agents can DECIDE, not just code.**
The whole lesson is a promotion: your agents stop being coding worker bees and become a **CEO and board** that answers your hardest strategic questions. Dan's category name: **agentic engineering**, not agentic coding. "Coding is just the beginning... it's the lowest hanging fruit."
*Why weak learners lose it:* they pattern-match to "another coding demo." It isn't — nothing gets coded here.

**2. Uncertainty in, decision out.**
Design any agent system by nailing input and output first. Here: **brief → deliberation → memo.** A structured question in; a ranked, dissent-annotated recommendation out. The debate is the workflow in the middle.
*Test yourself:* name the three nodes and which one is the "answer."

**3. The board's value is DISAGREEMENT.**
Eight specialists with controlled biases and opposing time horizons (Revenue: 90-day cash; Compounder: 24-month trust; Moonshot: 10x bet; Contrarian: attack assumptions). Their tension exposes flaws you can't see alone. A room that agrees added nothing.
*Say it Dan's way:* "multiple perspectives that don't agree so we can flesh out the mental model."

**4. Three innovations make it possible NOW.**
(1) **True 1M context** at flat price with graceful degradation — the enabler; (2) a **customizable agent harness (Pi)**; (3) **compounding agent expertise**. If you can only justify one as the unlock, it's 1M context: "the core four just got a massive buff."

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. A brief is validated — bad prompts don't run.**
Every brief must contain **## Situation, ## Stakes, ## Constraints, ## Key Question** (case-insensitive). Miss one → the meeting is blocked with a fix-it notice. This *forces* prompt engineering as a pattern. "If you template your engineering, your agents can do exactly what you did."

**6. Context files ride along to every agent.**
Any `.md` in the brief directory except `brief.md` is a **context file**, preloaded (via Pi's `@file`) into *every* board member's window. So the whole board shares the same business-metrics.md / product-overview.md before debate starts. Drop only `brief.md` and you've starved the board.

**7. Two custom tools run the meeting.**
`converse(to, message)` — broadcast ("all") or target members; returns their responses **plus a constraint-state block**. `end_deliberation(message)` — collect final statements and trigger the memo. That's the entire orchestration surface.

**8. The constraint engine bounds everything.**
After every `converse`, the CEO sees elapsed time + budget. At **80% of max** it starts wrapping; at max it sees **[MAX REACHED]** and *must* end. It also *can't* end before **min_time** (unless max is already hit). Budget counts every board cost **plus the CEO's own tokens**.

**9. CEO vs board are run differently.**
The **CEO is the Pi agent itself** (Opus 4.6; system prompt injected at `before_agent_start`). **Board members are separate `pi` subprocesses** with **persistent sessions** (`--session`), Sonnet 4.6 by default. First subprocess call sets `--system-prompt`/`--model` + preloads context; later calls reuse the session so context carries.

**10. The whole debate is logged (observability).**
Each meeting writes `conversation.jsonl` (from/to/message), `tool-use.jsonl` (every tool call), expertise updates, and argument SVGs. Replayable, auditable, improvable. "If you don't measure it, you cannot improve it. Full stop."

**11. Expertise compounds; memory doesn't.**
Per-agent scratch pads in `expertise/` **persist across deliberations** and grow (production files: tens of thousands of tokens). The revenue agent learns how to argue against the compounder; the CEO tracks which tensions resolved. The 1M window is what makes that practical.

**12. Skills bolt extra capability onto agents.**
The CEO's front matter lists `svg-generate` (decision-framework diagram) and `tts-eleven` (a 1–4 sentence ElevenLabs audio summary). Board members can also make argument SVGs. Skills are *paths + use-when* in the prompt — the agent reads and runs them itself.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing + the precise technical gotchas

**13. GOTCHA — "sequential" is a lie; converse is PARALLEL.**
`ceo.md` says board calls are "sequential — later members see earlier responses." The code runs them with `Promise.allSettled` (**parallel**), matching Dan's narration ("this runs in parallel... this isn't sequential"). Consequence: **within a round, members answer blind to each other**; they only build on each other **across rounds** by re-reading `conversation.jsonl`. Teach this mechanic explicitly.

**14. GOTCHA — "Contrarian speaks last" is NOT enforced (v1).**
The README and prompts promise Contrarian goes last. `end_deliberation` actually collects final statements in **config order** (Contrarian is 4th of 8) with no reordering. It's aspirational. Don't rely on ordering the code doesn't implement.

**15. Model versions are near-future placeholders.**
Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 / GPT-5.4 / Gemini 3.1 Pro are as spoken in a March-2026 recording. The book's baseline is newer (Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5). The tactic is model-agnostic — "the models must be able to maintain long context." Treat version strings (and the `/claude-.*-4-6/` "1M" badge regex) as period detail.

**16. The demo is all-Claude; diversity is the ideal.**
Dan: "agent model diversity is super super important for creating better conflict." But he runs the demo all-Claude (Opus CEO + Sonnet board) because other labs lacked true long context. The shipped `agents-multimodel` config already wires GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax, etc. via OpenRouter — the diversity path.

**17. It's one-shot, not a chat.**
`on('input')` blocks all typed text; ~20 built-in slash commands are shadowed. Only `/ceo-begin`, `stop`, `wrap` are honored. "This is not a conversation. This is a one-shot multi-agent system."

**18. Same brief, different vote — that's expected.**
On-screen TTS said "five to one"; the k8wlei memo says "7–1"; a scratch pad logged "6–2." Non-determinism is normal; Moonshot dissents consistently. Read variance as a feature of a real deliberation, not a bug.

**19. How much is a decision worth?**
Dan's framing question justifies the spend: size time + budget to the **value of the decision**, not to habit. The $1–$5 demo is deliberately tiny; production runs far higher. A good strategic call is worth far more than a few dollars and minutes.

**20. This is where vibe coders have no shot.**
Because you go down to the **system-prompt and subprocess primitives** — overriding the coding-agent persona, registering tools, spawning agents — you're building something a prompt-only user can't. "The awareness just isn't there."

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

1. State the system as a function in five words. Name its three nodes.
2. Name four board members and what each optimizes for. Why do you *want* them to disagree?
3. What are the three innovations, and which is the enabler — why?
4. Within one deliberation round, does a board member see the others' answers? Explain the mechanic.
5. What makes a brief valid, and what happens if it isn't?
6. Where do the prompts and the shipping code disagree — name both gaps.
7. How is the CEO run differently from a board member (agent vs subprocess, model, session)?
8. What forces a meeting to end, and when can the CEO *not* end early?

*(Answers: extract.md ideas 1–2, 4, 6, 3/12, 10, 12, 12, 5.)*

# MA-1 — Outdated vs Current (recording era → book build)

MA-1 was recorded ~March 2026 (briefs are dated 2026-03-17…22) and teaches primitives that age well, but it is closer to the frontier than the TAC lessons, so more of its *specifics* drift. For each item: what the lesson shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay or a callout. Two of these are not "aging" at all — they are **spec-vs-implementation gaps** a technical reader must know regardless of date.

---

## 1. Model versions: near-future placeholders that already drift  ⟵ period detail

**Recording era:** CEO on **Opus 4.6**, board on **Sonnet 4.6**; the retrieval chart benchmarks **Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro**; the multimodel config wires Qwen 3.5, Kimi K2.5, MiniMax M2.7, Xiaomi MiMo v2 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash.
**Current (book baseline):** the Claude line is newer (Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Haiku 4.5 / Fable 5). The exact strings — and the harness's `/claude-.*-4-6/` regex that stamps the "1M" TUI badge — are frozen at record time.
**Book treatment:** margin note on model-bearing frames ("version strings are period detail; the tactic is model-agnostic — 'the models must be able to maintain long context'"). Update the roster strings if reproducing.
**Overlay:** none.

## 2. 1M true context: headliner → table stakes

**Recording era:** framed as a fresh, singular unlock — "no model lab has been able to do this while maintaining a model that's actually useful"; flat price, no post-200K surcharge.
**Current:** long context at flat(ish) pricing is broadly available across labs by publish time; the "only Anthropic can do this" framing is a snapshot. The *pedagogy* holds — long context is what lets an agent hold a whole business + compounding expertise in one session.
**Book treatment:** "current practice" callout — keep the teaching (why long context enables the pattern), date-stamp the competitive claim, and re-check the retrieval-benchmark landscape before repeating "no one else can do this."

input.content:
# MA-1 Lab Spec — CEO Agents

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the **course codebase only** (`agentic-horizon-extras/ceo-agents`, symlinked as `ma-1-ceo-agents/codebase`). It is member-exclusive — no public clone. No external repos.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you build and change agents by **editing prompts, config, and briefs** — you author *briefs and system prompts*, not application code. The one code touch allowed is reading the extension to verify how it works (Part 4).
**Time box:** 60–90 minutes. **Token/$ cost:** 3–6 deliberations. Start with the demo's $1–$5 budget; raise it only for the "real decision" in Part 2 (size it to how much the decision is worth — that's the lesson).

Prereqs installed and keyed: **Pi**, **Bun**, **just**, `.env` with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (and optionally `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` for audio).

---

## 0 · Read the machine before you run it (10 min)

1. Boot: `just ceo` (or `j ceo`). Confirm the roster screen shows the CEO on `claude-opus-4-6` and the board on `claude-sonnet-4-6`, all badged **1M**, with the Time/Budget/Editor constraints. *(Frame `t0585`.)*
2. Open `.pi/ceo-agents/ceo-and-board-configuration.yaml` and answer **in writing**:
   - What are the min/max **time** and **budget**?
   - What four **required brief sections** must every brief contain?
   - How many **board members** are active, and what is each one's TUI color?
3. Open `.pi/ceo-agents/agents/moonshot.md` and name its `CORE_BIAS`, `RISK_TOLERANCE`, and `DEFAULT_STANCE`.

**Checkpoint 0 (graded):** without looking, state what the system takes in, what it returns, and the two ways a meeting can be forced to end (max time, max budget). If you can't, re-read — this is the "know your inputs/outputs/constraints" habit.

## 1 · Reproduce Dan — run a shipped brief (15 min)

1. `/ceo-begin` → select **`2026-03-18-acquisition-offer`**.
2. Watch a full deliberation. As it runs, note out loud:
   - the CEO's opening `converse("all", …)`,
   - the board **all responding at once** (parallel),
   - the **TIME/BUDGET gauges** advancing,
   - the moment **[MAX REACHED]** forces the wrap. *(Frames `t0760`, `t0900`.)*
3. When the memo opens in your editor, find: the ranked recommendation (#1–#3), the **board-stances table**, **Moonshot's dissent**, and the **next actions**. *(Frame `t0468`-style output.)*

**Checkpoint 1 (graded, write it down):**
- What did the board vote? (It will differ from the video's "5–1" — record *your* run's tally.)
- Which member dissented, and what did the dissent add to the memo that a single-agent answer would have missed?

## 2 · Author your own brief — a real decision (20 min)

1. Copy `.pi/ceo-agents/briefs/brief-template.md` into a new dir `briefs/<today>-<your-slug>/brief.md`.
2. Fill **all four** required sections for a decision you actually face (a tech-stack bet, a job offer, a pricing change). Be specific — "garbage in, garbage out."
3. Add **at least one context file** (`metrics.md`, `constraints.md`, whatever's relevant) in the same directory.
4. **Prove validation works:** temporarily delete your `## Constraints` heading, run `/ceo-begin`, and confirm the meeting is **blocked with a missing-section notice**. Restore it.
5. Raise `max_budget` in the config to a number that matches what this decision is worth to you, then run the deliberation.

**Checkpoint 2 (graded):**
- Your brief passed validation *only* after all four sections were present (you saw it fail, then pass).
- The memo references facts from your **context file** (proof it loaded into the board).
- One sentence: how did raising the budget change the depth of the debate?

## 3 · Customize the board (15 min)

Pick **one** (all via prompt/config edits, no app code):

- **3a — Bias a seat.** Edit one board member's `DEFAULT_STANCE` / `Reasoning Patterns` to sharpen its bias (e.g. make Contrarian even more adversarial). Re-run your Part-2 brief and show the changed stance in the new memo.
- **3b — Change the roster.** Comment a member out of the `board:` list (or add one back). Re-run and confirm the footer + memo reflect the new roster.
- **3c — Retune constraints.** Set `min_time_minutes` higher and re-run; show the deliberation refuses to end early until min time is met (the `end_deliberation` guard).

**Checkpoint 3 (graded):** the new memo/behavior demonstrably reflects your change, and you can point to the exact file + line you edited.

## 4 · Prove the technical truths from the logs (15 min)

1. Open the newest `deliberations/<your-slug>-<id>/conversation.jsonl`. Confirm every turn has `from` / `to` / `message`, bookended by `meeting_start` / `meeting_end`. *(Frame `t1420`.)*
2. Open `tool-use.jsonl` in the same dir — find at least one board member's tool call (a Read, or an SVG write).
3. **Parallel check:** in `conversation.jsonl`, look at one round. Note that board members' messages in the *same* round don't quote each other — they only reference prior rounds. Cross-check by reading `apps/ceo/extensions/ceo-and-board.ts` and finding `Promise.allSettled` in `converse`.
4. **Ordering check:** in `end_deliberation`, confirm final statements are collected in **config order** (Contrarian is 4th), *not* last — despite what `ceo.md` / `contrarian.md` claim.

**Checkpoint 4 (graded, one sentence each):**
- Why can two board members in the same round not have built on each other's arguments?
- Name the two places the prompts and the code disagree.

## Stretch (optional)

- **S1 — Model diversity.** Launch with the multimodel config (`ceo-and-board-configuration-multimodel.yaml`, agents in `agents-multimodel/`). Run the same brief and compare the debate's texture to the all-Claude run. *(Requires the relevant provider keys / OpenRouter.)*
- **S2 — Expertise persistence.** Run the same brief **twice**. Diff a member's `expertise/<member>-scratch-pad.md` before and after — show it accumulated notes. Explain why this compounds over 20 briefs.
- **S3 — Close the loop with a skill.** Ensure `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` is set and confirm the CEO speaks the memo (summary.mp3 saved beside the memo). *(Frame `t1052`.)*

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] Checkpoint 0: can state inputs, outputs, and the two forced-end conditions without notes.
- [ ] Ran a shipped brief end-to-end; recorded the vote tally and named the dissenter's added value (Checkpoint 1).
- [ ] Authored a valid 4-section brief **with a context file**; demonstrated validation *failing then passing* (Checkpoint 2).
- [ ] Made one board/config customization that visibly changed a subsequent memo (Checkpoint 3).
- [ ] Located `conversation.jsonl` + `tool-use.jsonl`; correctly explained the parallel-within-round mechanic and named the two spec-vs-code gaps (Checkpoint 4).
- [ ] Oral check, no notes: the three innovations and why 1M context is the enabler; two board tension-pairs; "uncertainty in, decision out"; and how you'd size budget to a decision's worth.

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **Most common stall:** trying to *type into* the meeting. It's one-shot — only `/ceo-begin`, `stop`, `wrap` are honored. If a student is "stuck," they're usually trying to chat.
- **Second stall:** a brief that won't run. 90% of the time it's a missing/renamed required section, or a context file that isn't `.md`. The blocking notice tells them exactly what's missing — teach them to read it.
- **Budget anxiety:** the demo's $1–$5 is deliberately tiny and produces a shallow memo. The *point* of Part 2 is to feel the difference when you size budget to the decision. If a student can't fund a single run, that budget conversation is the lesson surfacing early.
- **Don't over-teach the harness internals.** Part 4 is a *verification* pass (read enough of `ceo-and-board.ts` to confirm two facts), not a code-modification exercise. Keep the primitive crisp: agents that decide, uncertainty in / decision out.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** building a new Pi extension from scratch, RPC/SDK embedding, or multi-vendor tuning at depth — those belong to later Pi/agent-experts material.
